title: Your Office Isn’t Spy Proof
content: Welcome, Weekenders! A song has been stuck on loop in my mind for days now. Yeah, this one . C’mon, haven’t you heard the big, brassy James Bond theme playing too? We have an honest-to-goodness spy scandal on our hands! That would be the affair over at OpenAI, where the FBI has arrested a former engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, for allegedly placing a toilet paper–wrapped recording device in a conference room. Why’d he do it? The Justice Department wasn’t explicit in its press release announcing Alfozan’s arrest, though the statement does make sure to prominently describe him as a “national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” implying, obviously, that he was hoping to spy on OpenAI for the Saudis. I expect a not unsizable part of Silicon Valley experienced some schadenfreude when reading about the turn of events at OpenAI. I’d advise against indulging in that feeling, because when I struck up conversations with a few corporate security consultants and surveillance experts over the last few days, they all echoed the same sentiment: Plenty of companies risk ending up in the same situation—especially as they move quickly in today’s era of frenzied, heightened competition. A discomforting thought, eh? “Organizations can sometimes be moving so fast that they often don’t understand that there’s an issue associated with somebody until that person’s on board and up to no good,” said Bill Priestap, a former head of FBI counterintelligence who now runs his own security consultancy, Trenchcoat Advisors. “Meaning they’re recruiting, and they’re under such pressure to get the right people and get them on board that in many regards, they end up with a minimal understanding of the people they’re bringing on board.” Well, good thing there hasn’t been an enormous, frantic hiring binge lately. Ha ha ha. If you’re starting to feel a little paranoid, I strongly, strongly advise against talking to someone like David Abbott, a San Francisco private detective, to find out how easy it is to bug an office. Such conversations will only further unnerve you—you might end up holding your next board meeting in your home basement, Tony Soprano style—because according to Abbott, it’s pretty darn easy to install a recording device. A suitable one can be bought for less than $100. Some of the popular ones resemble phone chargers, which get tucked into a power socket, hidden in plain sight. He’s also seen surveillance devices in fake coffee cups—you know, like the ones that might lie casually around an office—and quite a few in fake smoke alarms. More bad news: Should you find such a device, it’s like spotting an ant in your kitchen. One ant suggests the presence of more ants. “If I’m doing a bug sweep, just because I find one does not mean there isn’t a second,” said Abbott. “If you find one, there’s going to be two. If you find two, there’s going to be three. You just keep looking.” What happened at OpenAI underscores Abbott’s warning. There, Alfozan, the alleged spy, did plant two bugs. Well, he tried to do so. Alfozan, not the sort who seems like he would’ve ever earned double 0 status, had placed another bug in a bag that he then mislaid: He reported it missing and had to go pick it up from the company’s lost and found. OK, if I’ve spooked the heck out of you, I guess I can offer some solace by pointing you in the direction of Eric and Greg Levesque, whose Salt Lake City–based startup, Strider Technologies, has raised $110 million in the last few years to sell AI-powered software to businesses that monitors email and other internal communications, flagging suspicious behavior and possible espionage attempts. (Yes, the company’s name is a reference to Strider from “The Lord of the Rings,” the nom de cloak of Aragorn, the character Viggo Mortensen plays.) “What we’ve found is that companies are not always dealing with trained intelligence operatives. Like, they’re dealing with scientists or legitimate engineers who have been approached or coerced in some form or fashion and are now working on behalf of someone else,” said Greg Levesque. “They can leave a lot of digital exhaust.” —Abram Brown ( abe@theinformation.com ) The Information’s Must-Read Stories Cursor Staff Investigated Whether Confidential Data Reached SpaceX for AI Training Anthropic’s Rapid but Slowing Growth Could Weigh on IPO Valuation Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst Race to Secure the Chips Their Startups Need How Microsoft’s New Office Chief Fixed Copilot and Won Over Nadella Listening: “ Reaching Out ” As the pandemic shut down the world in 2020, Sayre Quevedo, then a producer for The New York Times’ “The Daily” podcast, quit his job and headed out to Los Angeles, hoping for a chance at self-reinvention. To cope with those tumultuous times, he decided to pursue a documentary project, recording every phone call. Had nothing else of import happened in his life, Quevedo might’ve wound up with an intriguing time capsule. But something quite unusual did occur: Just months after moving to LA, he and his twin brother, Connor, happened to finally locate their biological father, whom they’d never before met. He worked as a barber—blocks from where Sayre lived. “Reaching Out,” a new podcast co-produced by NPR station KCRW that won a top prize in the Tribeca Festival’s expanded podcast categories, is a starkly intimate account of their journey to meet him and their reconciliation with each other, their lives and what life might’ve been like if their father hadn’t been a total stranger who happened to be just down the street. —Abram Brown Reading: “ Sitcom ” by Chuck Lorre and “ Emperor of Nothing ” by Blake J. Harris Chuck Lorre, the indefatigable TV showrunner, writer and producer, has kept the masses laughing for years—and years—and years, with a list of hits that includes “Two and a Half Men,” “The Big Bang Theory” and “Dharma and Greg.” Those are sitcoms, a term Lorre acknowledges once made him practically break out in hives, since it was often used to cheapen what he sees as grueling, high-touch art. With spicy good humor, he reclaims the word in his new memoir about his time in Hollywood, “Sitcom.” “The truth is, making a live studio audience laugh for twenty-odd minutes every week, for twenty-two weeks, is incredibly hard and unbelievably stressful,” Lorre writes. “If you’re one of those people who insist on labeling all sitcoms as being cheap, juvenile and unsophisticated, well…all I can say is, blow me.” I’d say “Sitcom” functions as a good primer on managing talent, too, and Lorre attests to having learned the importance of keeping out of the way. “Creativity needs air to breathe,” he writes. To do the opposite risks turning a leader into “one of those plastic bags you get at the dry cleaners that can kill small children.” Lorre also takes the opportunity to set down what he sees as good comedy’s basic tenets and decry the medium’s basest impulse: to write only about stupid people doing stupid things: “A better, perhaps deeper means to achieving laughter involves pain and suffering.” Such a sentiment is most certainly shared by Larry David of “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” the subject of “Emperor of Nothing,” a biography that won his reluctant cooperation. (When author Blake J. Harris finally wore David down, Harris received a two-line email from him: “Oh Jesus. If we must.”) As with “Sitcom,” “Emperor of Nothing” charts a remarkable rise across Hollywood from an inauspicious start: Lorre was a wannabe musician before his TV run, while David was a little-known stand-up comic with an unremarkable series of TV writing jobs before co-creating “Seinfeld.” Like Lorre, David describes the process of penning comedy as an arduous affair. And by David’s own telling, the process of sitting down to write a new “Seinfeld” season would bring on full panic. “That always seemed like a daunting prospect,” he recalled. “Especially because all the good ideas were used up the year before.” Fortunately, David had his friendship with the show’s eponymous star, Jerry Seinfeld, one of many people within David’s orbit who gave interviews for “Emperor of Nothing.” “I would always say, ‘All we have to do is write today,’” Seinfeld said. Or as David recalled: “Jerry always talked me off the ledge.” —A.B. Watching: “ War ” No one does a charming, self-involved cad better than Dominic West, the British character actor who first washed ashore in America as “The Wire”’s Detective McNulty and then again in Showtime’s “The Affair” and in the final two seasons of “The Crown” as Prince Charles. In “War,” HBO’s new high-tension legal drama, he’s tech billionaire Morgan Henderson, a fellow championing a safer, more responsible social media—while embroiled in an increasingly messy divorce from his Hollywood star wife, Carla (Sienna Miller). Much of that mess is Morgan’s own doing: He looks wonderful in his Savile Row trousers—he just has trouble keeping them on. As Morgan and Carla gird for an extended battle, they assemble a posse of cutthroat attorneys, who find their impulsive clients constantly upending their carefully laid strategies. That flock of legal eagles includes a handsome rogue, Johnny (Archie Renaux), a lad from working-class south London who sees a chance to ascend by, uh, redefining zealous representation. Backstabbing and double crosses abound. —A.B.

title: Singapore’s DayOne Pushes Ahead With Data Center IPO Tied to TikTok
content: DayOne Data Centers, a Singapore-based data center operator gearing up for a multibillion-dollar initial public offering in New York, is little known to most U.S. investors. But its business is built on a much better known company: ByteDance . The TikTok parent company accounts for nearly 70% of DayOne’s revenue, according to two people with knowledge of DayOne’s operations. DayOne, which started as a Chinese data center company’s overseas business unit four years ago, has benefitted greatly from ByteDance’s rapid global expansion through TikTok. But that has also left it extraordinarily dependent on a single customer, which the company has acknowledged creates a significant risk for its business.

title: Redwood to repurpose end-of-life batteries from Rivian vehicles - electrive.com
content:
Rivian and Redwood Materials are expanding their existing partnership. In addition to providing stationary battery storage, Redwood will play a larger role in the future on behalf of Rivian in recycling production waste and reusing decommissioned EV batteries.
Image: Redwood Materials
Rivian has confidently stated that the partnership will establish Redwood as one of its “key partners to enabling end-to-end energy solutions”. Specifically, Redwood will collect end-of-life EV battery packs from Rivian via the company’s nationwide network of service centres and then “[evaluate] each battery pack to determine whether to repurpose it for energy storage – deployed directly at Rivian’s manufacturing facilities or at other locations – or to recycle it,” as explained in an accompanying announcement.
Redwood will also recycle battery waste generated during Rivian’s production processes. This expanded scope of the partnership builds on an existing collaboration announced in April 2026, which initially focused on a specific project: the
construction of 10 MWh of battery storage capacity
using unused Rivian battery packs at the EV manufacturer’s production plant in Normal.
The background is that Redwood shifted its strategic focus in 2025. Since then, while the company has continued to operate as a battery recycler for the recovery of critical raw materials such as cobalt, nickel, copper and lithium, it has increasingly invested
in the development and construction of stationary battery storage systems

title: New Siemens investment in Skeleton’s supercap tech to boost AI data centre services – Batteries International
content: Siemens has made a further undisclosed investment in supercapacitor firm Skeleton Technologies as part of a new ‘exclusive partnership’ for the German industrial group to expand in the AI factories sector. Under the partnership, announced on October 14, Siemens will have exclusivity in selling and scaling Skeleton’s products in the data centre market. Siemens has been involved with Skeleton as a tech partner since 2022 and as an investor from 2023. Strengthening their relationship will support an expansion of Siemens’ services from grid connection to AI racks — specialised server racks designed to support high-performance computing. New services offered under the agreement will resolve a key constraint on the expansion of data centres — the massive, rapid and recurring swings in electricity demand, the partners said. AI workloads synchronise thousands of powerful chips, whose power demand can rise or fall within milliseconds and aggregate into swings at megawatt scale in seconds. Skeleton said its supercapacitors solve this challenge by absorbing rapid power swings, protecting valuable equipment and the grid while helping operators increase processing capacity and limiting the need for costly and time-consuming upgrades to existing facilities. Peter Koerte, a member of Siemens managing board and the group’s president of smart infrastructure, said the race to scale AI is increasingly becoming a race for power. “By combining Siemens’ electrical infrastructure expertise with Skeleton’s breakthrough supercapacitor technology, we can help customers unlock more AI capacity, improve resilience and accelerate growth in a rapidly expanding market.” Skeleton CEO and co-founder Taavi Madiberk said: “This winning combination gives us the strongest value proposition in the AI power infrastructure market, and we plan to become the world’s largest provider of white-space power systems for AI data centres.” Skeleton announced last year that proprietary new ‘curved graphene’ tech had the ability to reduce data centres’ AI energy consumption by up to 45%, tackling a key challenge for expansion of AI systems. The firm has said previously its supercapacitors use no lithium, cobalt, manganese, or other critical raw materials, and are based on its tech. Batteries International reported in November 2025 on Skeleton’s formal opening of its €50 million ($58 million) SuperBattery factory in Finland. The firm said the plant, with a 1GW annual capacity, was Europe’s first producing high-power batteries for AI data centres. title: EnerSys names Grewal to lead digital, AI and cyber security strategy – Batteries International
content: EnerSys has appointed Navi Grewal as chief digital, AI and information officer. The lead and lithium battery major said on October 16 Grewal will lead the company’s global digital, AI, information technology, cyber security and enterprise data strategy. Her responsibilities will include modernising global business systems, boosting digital systems and establishing an enterprise AI strategy, with an emphasis on secure and reliable technology operations, data and automation. EnerSys said Grewal joins the company with nearly three decades of experience leading technology organisations and enterprise transformation across global industrial, manufacturing and consumer businesses. Her career to date has included posts at DuPont and the Exelon Corporation. She will report to president and CEO Shawn O’Connell and be a member of the EnerSys executive leadership team. O’Connell said: “As we continue executing our strategy to simplify operations, improve productivity and strengthen how we leverage technology, data and AI across the organisation, Navi will play an important role in helping us enhance decision-making and drive operational excellence across our business.” EnerSys revealed earlier this year it was realigning its previous four operating units into a three-segment operating model to boost organisational focus and better serve customers. The battery maker also announced refocused plans for its $500 million battery cell gigafactory in South Carolina for US defence needs — ending a tech partnership with French Li cells developer Verkor. title: BCI to develop US Li forklift battery safety programme – Batteries International
content: Battery Council International has been selected to develop a US government-backed national training programme for lithium forklift battery safety. BCI said on October 13 it had been selected by the Department of Labor’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) to develop the new safety training programme on lithium ion battery hazards for forklifts and other industrial material handling equipment. An OSHA funding award under the agency’s Susan Harwood Training Grant Program will provide financial support to BCI, whose recently formed industrial motive power lithium sub-committee will build the programme to help warehouses transitioning to modern battery-powered forklift technology. The ‘Battery Hazards Training for Industrial Material Handling Equipment’ project will produce classroom-quality, instructor-led training for workers and employers in warehousing, distribution, and industrial operations. BCI said training will be designed specifically for workplaces that are deploying lithium-powered forklift fleets, either as a conversion from internal combustion engines or in addition to existing lead battery powered forklifts. Critical safety information will also be provided to workers in training to maintain those fleets. Once reviewed and approved by OSHA, materials will be available at no cost to employers and workers across the US. Engineering experts from leading BCI member manufacturers including Crown Battery, East Penn Manufacturing, EnerSys, Stryten Energy, Sunlight Batteries and others will support the project. Final materials will be validated through a four-hour pilot training for 20 workers and employers at a member-affiliated facility operating a lithium ion or mixed forklift fleet, with the full project running through September 2027. BCI said it currently represents nearly every US forklift battery manufacturer, across both lead and lithium power, which has allowed the trade body to become an authority on material handling issues related to battery-powered equipment — from setting standards and test specifications to gathering shipping statistics to advocating on behalf of the industry. The move comes as the material handling industry is in the middle of a major transition, BCI said. Combustion engine forklifts are increasingly rare as battery power has become commonplace and fleets are increasingly adding lithium battery powered vehicles to the mix. Existing safety training was built largely around internal combustion engines and lead batteries, while lithium ion batteries come with unique safety requirements. BCI said the current forklift marketplace also comes with the potential for confusion as ‘lithium ion’ batteries include a variety of distinct chemistries, including LFP, NMC and NCA, each with its own thermal behaviour, charging profile and safety needs. Facilities running mixed fleets face the particular risk of applying assumptions from one battery type to another, BCI said. The new curriculum that will be created by BCI will complement existing industrial truck operator training available from OSHA. Planned training modules include: Lead acid charging hazards and controls, including hydrogen gas, ventilation, and electrolyte safety; Lithium ion charging hazards and controls, including thermal runaway warning signs, battery management systems, charging, storage, and handling damaged batteries; Managing mixed fleets and emergency responses, comparing an acid spill response with a lithium ion thermal event and coordinating with local fire departments. Courtney Greco, BCI’s director of technical programs and the project director for the grant, said: “The companies that design, build, and service forklift batteries understand these hazards better than anyone, and there’s no better forum for cross-company collaboration than BCI.” BCI president and executive director Roger Miksad said: “For decades, BCI and its members have written the playbook on forklift battery safety. Now, with OSHA’s backing via the Susan Harwood grant award, we have been selected to write the next chapter.” The post BCI to develop US Li forklift battery safety programme appeared first on Batteries International .

title: EU unveils new battery material projects to challenge China’s supply chain dominance – Batteries International
content: The EU has rolled out 46 new projects in its latest scramble to secure raw materials critical to battery manufacturing and other industries to counter China’s “weaponisation” of the sector. The European Commission announced extraction processing and recycling projects on October 9 for lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite and other materials — with others outside the EU to be unveiled soon. Industry commissioner Stéphane Séjourné said European companies need to produce regardless of external pressures, adding: “In an increasingly dangerous world, we want and need to be more independent.” His announcement came just days after fellow commissioner for climate, net zero and clean growth, Wopke Hoekstra, slammed China for using massive state subsidies and economic espionage to undermine Europe’s single market. Séjourné said China’s announcement in October 2025 of export restrictions on rare earths had the potential to shut down entire production chains in Europe, in the automotive industry or impact wind turbines. The implementation of some of those measures has been suspended and the EU continues to discuss the issue with China, but “this respite must now become a lasting security”, Séjourné said. The new projects are in addition to 47 others, adopted by the Commission last year. They will be spread across Belgium, Bulgaria, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Spain, and Sweden. Included are two projects on magnesium and three on tungsten to support defence and aerospace, with others on rare earth elements to support the permanent magnet value chain. Séjourné said all projects will bolster requirements set out in the EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act — ensuring that by 2030 capacity meets at least 10% of the bloc’s annual consumption for extraction, 40% for processing and 25% for recycling of strategic raw materials to enhance competitiveness, develop greater resilience and be less dependent on any single supplier. Last month, European clean transport campaign group, Transport & Environment, warned the bloc must establish a viable business case for domestic battery manufacturing immediately — or risk an exodus of capital and expertise to other countries in as little as three years. title: Swiss shares delisting blow for troubled ESS firm Leclanché – Batteries International
content: Swiss financial regulators are to delist all registered shares of energy storage company Leclanché in the latest blow for the troubled firm. The issuers committee of SIX Exchange Regulation, which regulates and monitors exchange participants and issuers on the Swiss Stock Exchange, announced the move on October 15 — after Leclanché missed a final deadline to publish its long-delayed annual report. Batteries International reported last month that Leclanché had filed a “precautionary” insolvency application for its two German subsidiaries, Leclanché GmbH and Leclanché Services GmbH, saying both units faced a cash shortfall. In its decision, SIX said the trading of shares in the Leclanché group will remain suspended until the announcement of definitive delisting. Following that announcement, there will be a three-month period during which trading will resume before the final trading day on the SIX Swiss Exchange. The brief trading period allows shareholders to exit on‑exchange before the listing is formally removed. Leclanché, which has 20 days to appeal the decision, said it continues to pursue short-term funding solutions to support the group’s going-concern requirements. The firm said it is in active discussions with customers that have indicated a willingness to provide further support, as well as with strategic partners and potential investors. Leclanché said: “The company’s customer order book remains strong and has grown in recent months. While Leclanché maintains a positive long-term outlook, it continues to face significant short-term financing, cash and production-capacity constraints. The company is working closely with partners to address its funding needs.” The post Swiss shares delisting blow for troubled ESS firm Leclanché appeared first on Batteries International .

title: ArcActive showcases lead acid tech in Australia ESS pilot – Batteries International
content: New Zealand-based ArcActive has launched a lead acid battery pilot project in Australia to demonstrate how the technology can make energy storage accessible and affordable for commercial and industrial firms. The pilot, at Deakin University’s renewable grid-connected battery testing facility on its Waurn Ponds campus, forms part of the university’s renewable energy microgrid. ArcActive CEO and MD Stuart McKenzie said in an article shared on LinkedIn on October 14 the system, supported by Australian energy firm Origin Energy, uses a redesigned internal battery structure, incorporating a fabric framework to support the material responsible for storing and releasing energy. McKenzie said the company aims to extend battery cycling life while retaining the lower cost associated with lead acid technology. The pilot seeks to address costs beyond the battery itself, including engineering, approvals, insurance and safety requirements. McKenzie said the system targets companies that could use battery storage to retain solar electricity for later use and reduce their reliance on grid power during periods of high prices. Lead acid technology could provide a familiar starting point for installations, as engineers, approval authorities and insurers already had experience with the technology, McKenzie said. “We want businesses to be able to deploy storage through a more standardised, repeatable process, with greater confidence about the cost, the approval requirements and the financial return.” Earlier this year, ArcActive was among companies taking part at the ELBC 2026 lead battery technical conference, which showcased innovations shaping the future of the industry. title: Exide Technologies introduces LFP BESS for business ‘energy resilience’ – Batteries International
content: Lead and lithium battery producer Exide Technologies has unveiled an LFP powered modular BESS, Solition Powerflex, offering what the firm said is a scalable storage system to give businesses energy resilience. The BESS has modular architecture supporting the connection of up to 15 units in parallel, providing a scalable solution for commercial and industrial facilities, e-mobility infrastructure, renewable energy projects, agriculture and biogas applications. Exide said on October 12 each unit delivers 125kW of power and 261kWh of energy capacity, with an integrated battery and power conversion system and plug-and-play design for fast deployment. The BESS comprises liquid cooling, integrated fire suppression and advanced monitoring capabilities. Powerflex incorporates a European-built storage control system which Exide said provides a single platform for connecting energy storage with site operations, generation systems, grid operators and market participants. The system also supports applications including peak shaving. Serge Arbes, Exide’s senior business director for global energy solutions, said: “Organisations are increasingly seeking to improve energy resilience, integrate renewable generation and optimise energy costs. Solition Powerflex has been designed to address these evolving requirements.” Earlier this year, Exide hailed key milestones achieved in emissions reduction and recycling in its latest sustainability report, after being re-awarded a gold award from global business sustainably rating provider, EcoVadis. title: EnergyX agrees 10-year lithium offtake deal with Trafigura – Batteries International
content: Extraction and refining tech company EnergyX has signed a definitive 10-year offtake agreement with commodities multinational Trafigura for a total 100,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium. EnergyX, formally known as Energy Exploration Technologies, said on October 13 the deal is worth more than $2 billion in revenue for EnergyX projects across lithium carbonate coming from its Project Black Giant in Chile and lithium hydroxide from Project Lonestar in Texas. Trafigura will take 66% of phase one offtake from Black Giant and 30% of phase one from Lonestar. Meanwhile, EnergyX is in talks with additional prospective buyers to reach 80% offtake as it moves toward commercial-scale production in 2028. The agreement supports EnergyX’s financing activities — with offtake being a key requirement for a $690 million letter of intent from the US Export-Import Bank and additional project finance lenders. EnergyX said the deal is a turning point for the firm, after proving its technology at pilot scale in a laboratory and at the company’s demonstration plants in the US and Chile, each of which it claims are the largest direct lithium extraction plants (DLE) in the respective countries. EnergyX’s production will be powered by its proprietary GET-Lit DLE and refining technology. “Offtake agreements are among the most important steps in taking a lithium project from development to production,” said Teague Egan, CEO of EnergyX who founded the company in 2018. “A long-term purchase commitment from a counterparty of Trafigura’s scale and credit quality shows that the market wants EnergyX’s product. It also gives lenders and investors the revenue visibility they need before committing capital to commercial construction.” Earlier this year, Italian energy giant Eni made a $225 million investment for a minority stake in Project Black Giant. EnergyX said in July the project, with planned capacity to produce up to 52,500 tonnes of lithium carbonate annually across the first two phases, was set to make it one of the largest lithium producers globally, as well as a world-leading direct lithium extraction technology manufacturing company. The Chile investment boost came after EnergyX was selected to develop and operate a lithium processing facility on a US army base, in a first for a military installation in the country. title: This Week's Top Five Stories in Supply Chain
content:
This Week's Top Five Stories in Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
CMA CGM operates a number of LNG-fuelled low carbon container feeder vessels in Northern Europe. Credit: CMA
This week's biggest stories feature a biofuel target, plans for a battery supply chain and discussions on pharmaceutical logistics challenges
DSV and CMA CGM target 12,000t ACT+ CO2 cut
In October, liner operator CMA CGM announced that it had signed a deal with DSV to reduce DSV’s CO2 emissions by 12,000 tonnes using a second generation UCOME biofuel.
DSV currently offers low carbon fuel options to its aviation and shipping customers, as well as a book-and-claim based offset model for its road logistics customers to make low-emission logistics easier and more accessible.
While the volume of UCOME based biodiesel required for the deal has not been disclosed, Supply Chain Digital notes that a similar deal between CMA CGM and DHL in December 2025 indicated that an estimated 25,000t of CO₂e well-to-wake emission reductions would require 8,990t of UCOME second-generation biofuel.
CEVA Names Leaders for Freight and Contract Logistics Arms
CEVA Logistics is restructuring its global operations, simplifying the company’s structure by establishing two business units, Freight Management and Contract Logistics.
The organisational restructure is intended to simplify decision-making, strengthen regional accountability and to bring the company’s operational leadership closer to customers. The changes lay the groundwork for the company’s next phase of growth under CEO Patrick Moebel.
Patrick said: “CEVA has extraordinary people, strong capabilities and an
unmatched global network
. Our focus is straightforward: empower our people, execute for our customers and deliver sustainable performance. Everything we are doing is designed to help our teams better serve customers around the world.”
DHL is expanding its healthcare logistics capabilities with new trade corridors. Credit: DHL
DHL Connects New Global Healthcare Supply Chains
In a market where reliability and access are key to operations, DHL Global Forwarding is
expanding its cold chain network
The introduction of six new corridors will result in greater connectivity between Europe, North America and Asia.
According to DHL, this will lead to a strengthened connectivity between supply chains, resulting in more reliability, consistency and risk mitigation.
PowerCo has experience operating Gigafactory production facilities in Salzgitter, Germany. Credit: VW Group
Volkswagen, PowerCo and Gotion Plan Battery JVs
Volkswagen and Chinese battery cell supplier Gotion High Tech have announced a deal as part of which the two companies will build
battery gigafactories
in Spain and Slovakia alongside a cathode production plant in Morocco.
The agreement between Volkswagen, its battery-focused subsidiary PowerCo and Gotion High Tech was announced in late September. As part of the agreement, the two companies will invest EUR3.22 billion (US$3.7 bn) in two battery production facilities in Spain and in Slovakia in late September 2026, as well as an LFP (lithium-iron-phosphate) cathode production facility in Morocco. Gotion is investing approximately EUR1.598bn in total.

Cencora: Visibility and Risk in Pharmaceutical Supply Chains
Supply chains are continuously facing disruption and risk in today's world. Internal pressures and external pressures are at high, driven by an ageing workforce, a growing skills gap and worsening climate pressures.
In pharmaceutical supply chains, demand is warring with resilience. These supply chains must run with extreme precision, operating
under strict temperature-controlled conditions
, being delivered without delay and reducing waste.
Brent Wilhelm,  Senior Vice President of Supply Chain Planning & Optimisation at Cencora, oversees supply chain design and strategy at the organisation. With this, he is working towards continuous improvement, integrated business planning and thorough transportation capabilities.

title: Here are the best electric bikes you can buy at every price level in October 2026
content:
I’ve spent countless hours here at Electrek doing detailed hands-on testing of hundreds of electric bikes. Through thousands of miles of riding, I’ve been fortunate to learn these e-bikes inside and out, top to bottom and front to back. That long-term experience with real-world e-bike testing has helped me find the best electric bicycles on the market for just about any budget.
Below are some of the top e-bikes I’ve hand-tested for every price range, current as of October 2026. Fall weather is upon us, bringing cooler temps and beautiful views, so it’s a great time to hop in the saddle and get out there riding! Check out the awesome e-bikes below, any one of which could become your next electric bike.
This list is divided into several price ranges. We’ll start with the best e-bikes under $1,000, then move on to the under-$2,000 category, under-$3,000 category, etc. The goal is to highlight some of my favorite models in various budget ranges to help you make the right decision based on your needs and budget.
Best electric bikes under $1,000
The sub-$1,000 electric bike category is critical for a few reasons.
First, it’s pretty hard to produce a quality e-bike and sell it for under $1k. Most of the options in this price category make too many sacrifices in quality or longevity to earn a spot on this list as one of “the best.”
Second, many newly curious e-bike buyers just aren’t prepared to drop several thousand dollars on a brand-new concept, making this price range critical for many new e-bike shoppers.
Fortunately, we’ve found some excellent options for cheap electric bikes that can still save you some serious dough.
Lectric XP LITE 2.0
The Lectric XP LITE 2.0 was recently updated and is now quite likely the king of bang-for-your-buck electric bikes.
For years, the $999 Lectric XP 3.0 has reigned supreme in the budget electric bike category. That’s still a great bike, and we’ll discuss it next, but the more affordable $799 Lectric XP LITE 2.0 is an even more wallet-friendly electric bike.
That new e-bike offers some great riding at under 800 bucks.
It’s a throttle-enabled Class 2 folding electric bike with 20″ wheels, a max speed of 20 mph (32 km/h) and a motor rated for 300W continuous and 819W peak. It’s not going to be the strongest hill climber, but it does get going quickly on flat and modestly hilly terrain.
And the biggest upgrades include hydraulic disc brakes as well as an optional Gates carbon belt drive system for an extra $100. Riders can also opt for a nearly double-sized battery for an extra $200.
This is the only e-bike in this price range that I know of with a 48V electrical system. All the other budget e-bikes under $800 use a 36V system and thus suffer from weaker power.
There are some things that you give up with this model, such as that the fenders aren’t included free. But for just $799, you’re still getting built-in lights, a hidden battery, large color LCD display and a lightweight folder. Plus it comes in five color options.
There’s a lot of value there!
Lectric XP LITE 2.0 quick specs
- Motor: 300W (819W peak) geared rear hub motor
- Top speed: 32 km/h (20 mph)
- Range: Claimed up to 72 km (45 mi) or 130 km (80 mi) with long-range battery)
- Battery: 48V 7.8 Ah (375 Wh)
- Weight: 22 kg (49 lb)
- Price: $799
Lectric XP4
The Lectric XP4 recently launched, replacing the Lectric XP 3.0 which was the previously undisputed best-selling electric bike in the US. The XP4 is expected to quickly take its title, racking up massive sales figures as riders flock to its extreme bang-for-your-buck. Simply put, it’s hard to find any other e-bike that offers this level of value!
The XP4 can get riders up to 28 mph (45 km/h) and now comes in either a 500W or 750W version, with respective battery sizes of 48V 10.4Ah and 48V 17.5Ah. The long-range version’s premium price tag ($1,299 vs the standard range model at $999) is perhaps even higher value than the already impressive base model.
Other upgrades include a new stronger rack design, torque sensor for smoother pedal assist, and improved hardware like the 8-speed transmission, hydraulic disc brakes, updated urban/trail hybrid-style tire tread, and a beautiful new TFT color screen.
The XP4 is hands-down the highest value e-bike I’ve ever tested and it’s quite obvious just how much time and effort went into building such a potent e-bike designed to fit so many different riders and tasks.
It’s hard to find a better combination of low cost and high performance anywhere in the e-bike market right now.
Lectric XP4 quick specs
- Motor: 500W or 750W geared rear hub motor (peaks at ~1,000W and ~1,300W)
- Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
- Range: 45-85 miles (70-135 km) depending on battery choice
- Battery: 48V 10.4Ah (500 Wh), or larger 17.5Ah (840Wh) battery choices available
- Weight: 69-71 lb (31-32 kg)
- Price: $999
Ride1Up Portola 02
When Ride1Up launched the original Portola, it was pretty obvious what the game plan was: fire a shot across Lectric Ebike’s bow with a direct competitor to the Lectric XP line. By all accounts, Ride1Up nailed it with an impressive competitor. Now the company has come back with the next generation of the bike, this time attempting to take on both the XP line and XP Lite from Lectric. That’s thanks to two models, the Portola 02, and the stripped down Portola 02 Lite.
The Ride1Up Portola 02 has a lot more going for it than just the attractive starting price of $895 for the Lite or $995 for the full-size bike with frame-integrated rack. The models offer great performance with a maximum speed of 28 mph (45 km/h) and good quality components including hydraulic disc brakes, torque sensor, front suspension, a built-in rear rack (except for the Lite), and a 750W motor.
There are two battery options available, either a 48V 10Ah or a 48V 15Ah, and the larger battery only costs an extra $100, so it’s quite worth the extra 50% range.
I love the sleek-looking frame and apparently, I’m not alone. Those who are on the hunt for a good-looking folding fat tire e-bike that doesn’t break the bank will likely find this to be one of the more fashionable options.
Ride1Up Portola 02 quick specs
- Motor: 750W geared rear hub motor
- Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
- Range: Claimed up to 72 km (45 mi), but less if you’re heavy on the throttle
- Battery: 48V 10 Ah (480 Wh), or larger 48V 15 Ah (720 Wh) battery available
- Weight: 26-28.5 kg (58-63 lb depending on options)
- Price: starting at $895
Best electric bikes under $2,000
Once you bump up above the $1,000 limit, you start to see many more great options for e-bikes in a wide range of categories.
JackRabbit OG2 micro e-bike
The $1,249 JackRabbit OG2 is in one of these fuzzy areas between e-bikes and other e-rideables. In this case, it straddles the line between an electric bike and an electric scooter.
It more or less feels like an electric bike based on its ride geometry. However, the lack of pedals means that it could also be classified as an electric scooter, albeit a large-wheeled e-scooter.
But with those 20-inch wheels and bicycle seat, the JackRabbit OG2 rides much more like a small folding e-bike than an e-scooter. And its electronics match that of a light e-bike, too.
The 300W motor gets the little runabout up to 20 mph (32 km/h). The small 158 Wh battery only offers around 10 miles (approximately 16 km) of range, but is also conveniently small enough to easily keep a spare battery in a cargo pocket or even a small purse.
The biggest benefit of the JackRabbit is that it is so simple that the lack of frills keeps the weight down to just 25 lb (11.3 kg)! For an e-bike, that’s almost so light that it floats.
The company also released a higher power and larger battery capacity version too, which might be good for riders who want to push harder and go farther. For those that want to see a few more upgrades on this minimalist e-bike, the JackRabbit OG2 and XG might be more your size.
See my full review of the JackRabbit OG2 here.
JackRabbit OG2 quick specs
- Motor: 300W geared rear hub motor
- Top speed: 32 km/h (20 mph)
- Range: 20 km (12 mi)
- Bike weight: 11.3 kg (25 lb)
- Brakes: Rear mechanical disc brake
- Price: $1,249
Lectric XPedition 2.0
We called the Lectric XPedition e-cargo bike a runaway success right from the start, and that’s exactly what it turned into. Now with the new Lectric XPedition 2.0 on the road, it’s better than ever.
With heavy-hauling weight capacity, the option for one or two batteries for extra long range, hydraulic disc brakes and torque sensor-based intuitive feeling pedal assist, this e-bike is dragging electric cargo bikes into the future.
The $1,399 Lectric XPedition 2.0 has turned the electric cargo bike market upside down, bringing a heavy-hitting cargo e-bike to market for an ultra-affordable price.
While it’s not the fanciest cargo e-bike on the market (you’ll find those in the $4,000-$6,000 price range further down this article), it’s definitely the best bang for your buck thanks to a combination of high value parts and reasonable pricing.
Lectric XPedition 2.0 quick specs:
- Motor: 750W rear hub motor
- Battery: 48V 14Ah (672 Wh) with the option for a second battery (and higher capacity batteries)
- Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
- Range: up to 75 miles (120 km)
- Weight: 74 lb (33.5 kg)
- Price: $1,399
Heybike Ranger 3 Pro
The Heybike Ranger 3 Pro is probably one of the best deals in full-suspension folding e-bikes right now. With a combination of a powerful motor, comfortable geometry, front & rear suspension, and a high-tech interface that includes NFC card unlocking, the Heybike Ranger 3 Pro is punching above its weight class.
In fact, that’s its main drawback, its weight. It’s a heavy bike, but the speed and power mean heavier motors and batteries, so you know you’re going to be carrying a more robust powertrain around with you.
But between the performance and the looks, this is one awesome comfortable ride that just doesn’t break the bank! I had a blast reviewing it, and I’ll bet you’ll have a blast riding it!
Heybike Ranger 3.0 Pro quick specs
- Motor: 750W rear hub motor
- Top speed: 28 mph (pedal assist), 20 mph (throttle)
- Battery: 48V 15Ah (Samsung cells)
- Range: 55 miles (claimed), ~40 miles real-world
- Suspension: Front hydraulic fork + rear shock
- Price: $1,499
Aventon Soltera.2
The $1,399 Aventon Soltera.2 is the latest version of Aventon’s beautiful city bike that offers some of the best quality fabrication that I’ve seen in this price range – or even in higher price ranges. It is offered in either a single-speed or seven-speed format.
The bike rolls on narrow tires for that efficient city ride, while still packing in a 500W motor.
The battery is a bit smaller at 36V and 10Ah, but the bike makes up for a smaller battery by being able to integrate it into the frame in a sleek and attractive package.
The beautiful color display also adds to the bike’s charm, as do the powerful headlight and frame-integrated tail light. There’s even an awesome companion app that lets your phone track your bike’s important stats. Basically, you’re getting a lot for $1,199 here!
Check out my in-depth Aventon Soltera.2 review here.
Aventon Soltera.2 quick specs:
- Motor: 500W peak-rated rear hub motor
- Battery: 36V 10Ah (360 Wh)
- Top speed: 20 mph (32 km/h)
- Range: 20-63 miles (32-101 km)
- Weight: 46 lb (21 kg)
- Price: $1,199
Ride1Up Roadster V3
Ride1Up has proven itself as a high-value electric bike brand, focusing largely on efficient and speedy commuter e-bikes. While the company has many models in the $1,000 to $2,000 range, the $1,295 Ride1Up Roadster V3 is one of the best bang-for-your-buck options in the lightweight category.
This 500W-rated e-bike offers Class 3 performance, meaning you can hit speeds of up to 28 mph (45 km/h), or a still impressive 20 mph (32 km/h) if using the throttle. But sticking to pedal-assist means you get to enjoy that quality torque sensor for smoother pedaling. The bike even comes with an option for either a belt drive or a 10-speed Shimano transmission, and three frame sizes to choose from.
The V3’s design was updated with many new features, including a now-removable battery for even more convenient charging both on and off the bike. And with a sub-40 lb weight, it’s hard to beat this one on a pound-for-pound basis!
Ride1Up Roadster V3 quick specs:
- Motor: 500W rear hub motor
- Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
- Range: 32-64 km (20-40 mi) throttle vs. pedal assist
- Battery: 36V 10Ah (360 Wh) with genuine LG cells and UL certified
- Weight: 17.6 kg (39 lb)
- Price: $1,295
Check out my full review of the Ride1Up Roadster V3 here:
Lectric XPeak2
Lectric Ebikes expanded into larger territory with the launch of the Lectric XPeak2. It was the company’s first e-bike with a larger than 20″ wheel size, bringing some chunky 26×4.0″ tires into the company’s inventory.
The XPeak takes the form of a typical adventure-style fat tire electric bike. It features a hardtail design with a suspension fork, high-volume tires, hydraulic disc brakes, and a relatively large battery that is certified by the Swiss testing agency SGS to meet UL 2849 standards.
The bike is also tested to higher standards for ruggedness of the frame and fork than most e-bikes in this price range, meaning it’s likely going to last longer too. As far as fat tire adventure-style e-bikes go, there’s no better bang for your buck than the Lectric XPeak2.
Lectric XPeak2 quick specs:
- Motor: 750W (1,300W peak)
- Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
- Range: Up to 75 km (45 mi) on low power
- Battery: 48V 15 Ah (720 Wh)
- Weight: 39.4 kg (67 lb)
- Price: $1,499
Ride1Up Vorsa
The Ride1Up Vorsa is Ride1Up’s most versatile “SUV‑style” e‑bike yet, designed to transition seamlessly from commuting through city streets to loaded errands and light gravel or park paths. With a standard price around US $1,495, it delivers an exceptionally high‑value riding experience that often outperforms models far above its price range.
With a powerful 750 W rear‑hub motor producing a hefty 95 Nm of torque (and peaking over 1,400 W in real-world tests), the Vorsa accelerates comfortably and can maintain Class 3 speeds of up to 28 mph via pedal assist or 20 mph throttle thanks to its dual-sensor system and customizable display. Whether you’re hauling cargo or cruising commute lanes, the Vorsa delivers smooth, responsive power that feels natural and planted.
I love how well‑rounded the package is. Ride1Up outfits the Vorsa with a 100 mm suspension fork, comfortable ergonomic bars, multiple colors/frame styles (step‑thru or standard), and a modular rear rack rated for 440 lb total payload, which is expandable via Connect+ accessories. Hydraulic disc brakes, full fenders, integrated lighting, and passive features like UL‑certified batteries and Apple FindMy integration round out the build.
At just $1,695, the Ride1Up Vorsa is priced way below fair market value, which makes this an absolute steal of a deal.
Check out my Ride1Up Vorsa review here, and also check out the new expansion to the Vorsa line with lighter and heavier duty models built on the Vorsa platform.
Ride1Up Vorsa quick specs:
- Motor: 750W rear geared hub motor
- Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
- Range: 50-100 km (30-60 mi)
- Battery: 48V 15Ah (720 Wh)
- Weight: 29 kg (65 lb)
- Price: $1,495
Monarc Marker electric adventure bike
The Marker is the first model unveiled by the e-bike brand spun out of Lectric eBikes, known as Monarc. The brand leverages Lectric’s size and buying power to bring higher end bikes than we typically see in the budget space – complete with higher shelf components – but at better prices and with better customer service.
The Monarc Marker is a powerful, Class 3-capable fat tire adventure e-bike with powerful four-piston brakes, a quality reverse arch suspension fork, Shimano CUES transmission, and comes with two batteries, all for an incredible reasonable MSRP of US $1,999.
Monarc also made waves by offering a 5-year warranty as well as 12-hour customer service five days a week, ensuring customers feel comfortable knowing they are buying from a company that will stick around to support riders long after the purchase is complete.
Learn more about the Monarc Marker here, or check out its current sale price here.
- Motor: 750W (1,638W peak) rear-geared Bafang hub motor
- Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
- Battery: 2x 48V 15Ah (720 Wh) for a total of 1,440 Wh
- Range: Up to 40 miles (65 km) per battery, or 80 miles (130 km) with two batteries
- Price: $1,999
Juiced Scrambler
When Juiced returned with a vengeance after being saved by Lectric, the brand did so with two impressive new Scrambler models: a hard tail and a full-suspension bike. They’re both awesome moped-style e-bikes and handle great, but the full-suspension version definitely kicks things up a notch and allows for even wilder riding.
But since they share the same features and performance outside the rear suspension, either would make an awesome addition to your e-bike fleet. Basically, it’s a powerful yet street-legal e-bike that is designed for real-world riding, thanks in no small part to its designer, Austin Homes, being a seasoned competitive bike racer across multiple disciplines and bringing that keen eye to the Scrambler’s development.
Juiced Scrambler quick specs:
- Motor: 750W continuous-rated rear hub motor
- Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
- Range: Up to 60 miles (up to 98 km)
- Battery: 52V 19Ah (988 Wh)
- Weight: 83-85 lb (37.6-38.5 kg) for HT/FS, respectively
- Price: $1,699 (HT) or $1,899 (FS)
Best electric bikes from $2,000 to $3,500
If you’re spending this much, you’ll want to ensure you’re buying from a reputable company with top-notch products and service.
Ride1Up TrailRush
The Ride1Up TraiRush is the first actually quite good electric mountain bike that comes in at a budget price. It gives you a real German-made Brose motor, which offers good power matched with whisper-quiet performance. You get a dropper seat post and Maxxis Minion tires, Tektro Orion quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, and a 120mm Rockshox Judy Silver TK Air Fork.
The first time I took a ride on the Ride1Up TrailRush, I couldn’t believe just how good the bike felt, especially from a company known for its wide array of commuter and street-oriented electric bikes. But Ride1Up was founded by cyclists at heart, and so they know what it means to build a good bike, regardless of category. At $2,095, this is a steal for just great parts.
Ride1Up TrailRush quick specs:
- Motor: Brose TF Sprinter mid-drive
- Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
- Range: 30-50 miles (50-80 km)
- Battery: 36V 14Ah (504Wh)
- Weight: 57 lb (25 kg)
- Price: $2,095
Lectric One
The Lectric ONE is something of an enigma in the e-bike market. To put it into perspective, it’d be hard to buy the gearbox alone on this bike for under $2,000, and yet that’s nearly the price tag of the entire bike! For just $2,399, you’re getting an e-bike with components normally found on $10,000+ bikes.
The Lectric One was unveiled as a lightweight commuter e-bike designed with an ultra high-end drivetrain based around the Pinion C1.6i auto-shifting gearbox. Paired with a Gates carbon belt drive and a true 750W-rated Stealth M24 motor (with 1,300 peak watts!), the Lectric ONE hits class 3 speeds in style with some extra premium components.
Lectric ONE quick specs:
- Motor: 750W rear hub motor (1.3 kW peak)
- Battery: 48V 10.4 or 14Ah (500Wh or 672 Wh)
- Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
- Range: up to 75 miles (120 km)
- Weight: 55 lb (25 kg)
- Price: $2,399
Ride1Up Prodigy V2 mid-drive e-bike
The $2,295 Ride1Up Prodigy V2 has brought new meaning to the phrase “low-cost mid-drive electric bike”, updating an already impressive e-bike with a new next-gen setup.
This e-bike sports a high-end German-manufactured Brose mid-drive motor and can hit speeds of up to 28 mph (45 km/h), yet is price similarly to much cheaper hub motor-based electric bikes.
It’s a perfect commuter e-bike for someone who wants high-quality parts like that German mid-drive motor with 90Nm of torque, hydraulic disc brakes, bright LED lights, included fenders, rear rack, and a very comfortable saddle. Plus there’s a choice between a nice 9-speed chain drive transmission or a fancier Gates Carbon Drive belt setup with an Enviolo continuously variable transmission.
This e-bike is easily worth another $500 more than the price tag, if not more. In fact, you’ll find many of these same components on e-bikes with $3,000-$4,000 price tags all over the place. So if you’re looking for a higher quality e-bike that doesn’t cost as much as a fancy bike shop e-bike, this is the one to consider.
Ride1Up Prodigy quick specs:
- Motor: Brose TF Sprinter mid-drive
- Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
- Range: 30-50 miles (50-80 km)
- Battery: 36V 14Ah (504Wh)
- Weight: 58 lb (26 kg)
- Price: $2,395
Priority Current Plus
I love the $3,299 Priority Current electric bike so much that it has become one of my daily riders. It’s the one I grab when I’m doing city riding and I know I want to be pedaling.
While the original version was already a great bike, the new Current Plus adds some key improvements, such as an included throttle and a nearly 50% larger capacity battery for more range. The throttle is great in a pinch, but the bike is also just so much fun to pedal thanks to a torque sensor-based pedal assist that provides natural-feeling assistance up to a fast 28 mph top speed.
The internally geared rear hub combined with a Gates belt drive system and powerful hydraulic disc brakes make this a very nice e-bike for the price. Plus that mid-drive motor offers tons of torque (140 Nm!) for climbing hills or accelerating quickly.
I’m also a fan of the built-in lights and included fenders, not to mention the punchy hydraulic disc brakes and Goodyear tires.
Mid-drive electric bikes aren’t cheap, but the price is definitely a fair one for this e-bike.
Priority Current Plus quick specs:
- Motor: 500W mid-drive motor with torque sensor
- Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h) or 20 mph (32 km/h) user-selectable
- Range: 40-75 miles (64-120 km)
- Battery: 720 Wh frame-integrated battery
- Weight: 24 kg (53 lb)
- Price: $3,299
Ride1Up CF Racer1
I’m not normally a carbon fiber, drop bar, race bike kind of guy. But then again, that’s usually because those types of bikes are way out of my price range… until now.
The Ride1Up CF Racer1 brings carbon fiber road e-bikes to the common man, offering both a traditional road bike and a gravel bike edition.
At under 29 lb (13 kg), these e-bikes are some of the lightest around. I picked one up with my index finger and was shocked at how easily it left the ground.
To get there, that meant a relatively low-power motor and a smaller battery were required. But for the folks that ride these types of bikes, a big motor and heavy battery probably aren’t on their wishlist anyway. Instead, a simple extra boost, as if you’ve always got a tailwind, helps augment your own pedaling.
For just $2,295, there’s no better deal out there for a budget-friendly carbon fiber road e-bike.
Ride1Up CF Racer1 quick specs
- Motor: 250W 42 Nm torque
- Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h) on pedal assist
- Range: 16-40 miles (26-64 km)
- Battery: 252 Wh frame-integrated battery
- Weight: 12.9 kg (28.6 lb)
- Price: $2,295
Ride1Up REVV1 FS
This full-suspension electric moped-style e-bike is a masterclass in high performance electric bike design. Sure, it’s an obvious SUPER73 imitation, but it’s a really well done imitation.
It handles well, it’s got great rubber between you and the road, the suspension gives a comfortable ride, and it’s got plenty of extra power.
Despite the 750W label, the e-bike can be unlocked to make use of nearly 1,500W of peak power. I was able to reach a top speed of 37 mph (59.5 km/h) during my testing (not on public streets!).
But the bike ships in Class 2 mode with a 750W limit and 20 mph (32 km/h) maximum speed, meaning you’ll have to contact the company to request an unlock for the bike to be used above Class 2 speeds and power levels.
All in all, the $2,395 Ride1Up REVV1 FS is an amazing e-bike for anyone who wants a moped-style ride with full-suspension, high quality 4-piston hydraulic disc brakes and a design that rides almost like a motorcycle, yet in a bike form factor.
Check out my complete Ride1Up REVV1 FS review here.
Ride1Up REVV1 quick specs:
- Motor: Bafang 750W continuous rear hub motor
- Top speed: 20 mph (32 km/h) out of the box, 37 mph (59.5 km/h) when unlocked
- Range: 30-60 miles (48-96 km)
- Battery: 52V 20Ah (1,040 Wh)
- Weight: 93 lb (42 kg)
- Price: $2,395
Tern Quick Haul
The Tern Quick Haul is an electric cargo bike from the famed cargo e-bike company Tern. It holds the distinction of being the most affordable model in Tern’s lineup.
That says a lot, because Tern is known for its high-quality e-bikes that are built to be ridden every day for real-world errands, carpool duty, and more. These e-bikes are meant to replace cars, and they do just that for many riders. With a huge list of accessories, you can outfit a Quick Haul for just about any job.
The Tern Quick Haul features a mid-drive Bosch motor, hydraulic disc brakes, Tern’s vertical parking rack, and a relatively lightweight but high utility design that is meant to carry just about anything in your life.
We had the chance to test a pair of Quick Hauls at Eurobike in Frankfurt last year, which you can learn more about here.
Motor: Bosch Active Line Plus mid-drive motor
Top speed: 20 mph (32 km/h) with pedal assist (no throttle)
Range: Up to 60 miles (96 km), less when riding in highest power
Battery: 400Wh, removable/lockable
Weight: 50 lb (22.8 kg)
Price: $2,999
Ariel Rider X-Class
When it comes to fast, powerful electric mopeds on a budget, it’s hard to compete with the $2,399 Ariel Rider X-Class. This is the e-bike I usually recommend when someone simply wants the most power and speed for the least amount of money.
The impressive performance comes from a powerful 1,000W motor that actually puts out closer to 2,000W of peak power. It can be limited to 20 mph if you’d like, but I got it up to 36 mph in unlimited mode.
The bike rolls on 20″ moto-style wheels and comes with nice parts including hydraulic disc brakes, a bench seat, dual suspension, and a big moto-style headlight.
You can see my full review of the Ariel Rider 52V X-Class here.
- Motor: 1,000W (2,000W peak) rear hub motor
- Top speed: 36 mph (58 km/h), but can be limited to Class 2 speeds
- Range: Up to 75 miles (120 km), less when riding at top speed
- Battery: 52V 18Ah (936 Wh), removable/lockable
- Weight: 80 lb (36 kg)
- Price: $2,399
Xtracycle Hopper electric cargo bike
The Xtracycle Hopper is something of a Goldilocks cargo bike, in my opinion. It’s not as big as a traditional long tail cargo bike, but it’s still big enough to carry multiple kids or a week’s worth of groceries.
It’s also not as pricey as the expensive $5-7k bike shop cargo e-bikes, yet it’s much higher quality than the typical direct-to-consumer cargo e-bikes.
I’ve tested it for all sorts of cargo jobs and even put my friends and family on it to take their kids to school and let me know how it works for them. Everyone has come away impressed with the ride feel, which seems much more like a traditional bike than a bulky cargo bike.
For the money, the Xtracycle Hopper offers incredible value and much higher quality construction than you’d get with entry-level brands.
Check out my full Xtracycle Hopper review here.
Xtracycle Hopper quick specs:
- Motor: 750W geared rear hub motor
- Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
- Range: 32-80 km (20-50 mi) depending on throttle or pedal assist
- Battery: 48V 15Ah (720 Wh)
- Weight: 38.5 kg (85 lb)
- Price: $2,499
Best electric bikes from $3,500 to $5,000
Above $3.5k, you’re entering some seriously dedicated e-bike territory.
These e-bikes either feature top-shelf components like drivetrain and brake parts, or pack in so much power that they couldn’t possibly be priced any lower.
Either way, you’re not in Kansas anymore. You’re heading down the e-bike rabbit hole.
Tern HSD
Tern is renowned for building high-quality electric bikes that double down on utility features. The newly updated Tern HSD is the company’s more affordable utility e-bike, offering many features you’ll find on its higher-end GSD but at a price that more riders can stomach.
The HSD uses small 20″ wheels and includes a folding stem, making it nice and compact. But taking it one step further, Tern outfitted it with its innovative rack that lets you park the bike on its tail, meaning it takes up barely more space than a coat rack in the corner of a room.
The bike’s Bosch mid-drive and high capacity batteries provide a high-end e-bike drive, and they are matched with a variety of performance drivetrain options that you can select from, depending on how high you want to spec the bike.
Whether you’re ferrying around kids or buying a week’s worth of groceries, the HSD is a solid option.
Check out my detailed first ride experience on the Tern HSD here.
Tern HSD quick specs:
- Motor: Bosch Active Line Plus mid-drive
- Top speed: 32 km/h (20 mph) with electric assist
- Range: 42-110 km (26-69 mi) depending on pedal input
- Battery: Bosch PowerPack 400 Wh
- Weight: 25.4 kg (55.9 lb)
- Price: $4,299
CSC FT1000MD
The CSC FT1000MD sounds like a motorcycle name because it comes from a company with motorcycle heritage. CSC Ebikes was born out of CSC Motorcycles, a company with several decades of two-wheeler experience.
The FT1000MD is the company’s highest power option. The fat tire e-bike comes with a 1,000+ watt motor known as the Bafang M620 Ultra. It’s the most powerful and highest torque e-bike mid-drive motor on the retail market. CSC paired it with a big battery, quality suspension, hydraulic brakes, built-in lighting, and more to create a high performance and high-quality adventure e-bike.
I was able to hit speeds of around 34 mph with the motor in unlocked format, though you can limit it to 20 or 28 mph to fit into class 2 and class 3 designations.
Check out my full review of this incredibly powerful e-bike here.
CSC FT1000MD quick specs:
- Motor: 1,000W continuous Bafang M620 mid-drive
- Top speed: 54 km/h (34 mph) when unlocked
- Battery: 48V 16Ah (768Wh) with Samsung 35E cells
- Frame: 6061 aluminum
- Suspension: Front suspension fork with preload and damping adjustment, plus lockout
- Brakes: Tektro hydraulic disc brakes with 180 mm rotors
- Weight: 34 kg (75 lb)
- Price: $3,299 or save $200 with discount code ELECTREK
Ariel Rider Grizzly
When it comes to all-wheel-drive electric bikes, the $3,299 Ariel Rider Grizzly is one of my favorites.
This incredible e-bike is really more of a small electric motorcycle. It uses two high-power motors – one in each wheel – to offer speeds in the mid-30s and acceleration that will get you there in the blink of an eye.
Full suspension and hydraulic disc brakes make this an e-bike that handles well at any speed, and the bright red paint job looks as aggressive as the e-bike feels. It even comes with footpegs pre-installed so you can carry a passenger with you.
Plus it’s got double batteries to feed those two power-hungry motors, so you’ll be able to ride this e-bike pretty darn far too, as long as you aren’t too demanding from the throttle.
Check out my full in-depth review of the epic Ariel Rider Grizzly e-bike here.
Ariel Rider Grizzly quick specs:
- Motors: Dual 1,000W continuous hub motors (1,850W peak or 3.7 kW combined)
- Top speed: 36 mph (58 km/h) when unlocked, but can be limited to Class 2 speeds
- Range: Up to 75 miles (120 km), less when riding at top speed
- Battery: 52V 35Ah (1,820 Wh) between two removable/lockable batteries
- Weight: 105 lb (47.6 kg)
- Price: $3,299
Priority Skyline
The Priority Skyline builds upon Priority Bicycles’ legacy of creating high-performance, low-maintenance e-bikes and ups the ante with more premium parts than we’ve ever seen on a Priority e-bike before.
The show stopper here is the inclusion of Pinion’s 12-speed automatic gearbox, which smartly shifts gears without the rider ever having to think about it. You can personalize your shift points to dial in the ride, and let the centrally-mounted gearbox do the rest. The carbon belt drive transfers your pedal power while a 750W rear hub motor brings the extra power riders need.
There are also high-quality hydraulic brakes, a great suspension fork, and a big battery for long range in the city. Rear rack and complete fenders come standard, as do the built-in LED lights and adjustable handle-bar stem.
See my full review of the Priority Bicycles Skyline here.
Priority Bicycles Skyline quick specs:
- Motor: 750W hub motor with torque sensor
- Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
- Range: Up to 96 km (60 mi) on pedal assist, less on throttle
- Battery: Downtube-integrated and removable 720 Wh battery
- Weight: 30.8 kg (68 lb)
- Price: $3,999
Best electric bikes above $5,000
You just couldn’t stop, could you? I showed you plenty of awesome e-bikes that didn’t cost most of a paycheck. But you just haaaaaaad to keep going.
Fine, here they are. These are some of the most expensive e-bikes out there that we’ve tested and that I’d actually recommend someone buying, if you can pony up the cash.
GoCycle G4i+
When it comes to ultra-premium folding electric bikes, there’s only one name that comes to my mind: GoCycle. These are the most impressive folding e-bikes I’ve ever seen. And they better be – they were designed by a former McLaren engineer.
Between the carbon fiber work, single-sided wheels, high-tech tires, trippy LED dot display, innovative rear suspension, and completely enclosed drivetrain, there’s a lot of high-end stuff going on here.
The speed will vary from 15-20 mph depending on which country you buy the bike in, but the performance is only part of the equation. The quick folding and light, compact design of the e-bike is the real winner here.
Check out my full review of the GoCycle G4i+ here.
GoCycle G4i+ quick specs:
- Motor: 500W front hub motor
- Top speed: 20 mph (32 km/h) in the US
- Range: up to 50 miles (80 km)
- Battery: 36V 10.4Ah (375 Wh)
- Weight: 37.2 lb (16.9 kg)
- Price: $6,999
FREY EX Pro electric mountain bike
The FREY EX Pro is a high-end electric mountain bike with crazy high power. It uses the same motor as the CSC FT1000MD we featured above (the Bafang M620 mid-drive), but cranks up the current to provide closer to 1,500W of power.
It’s enough to destroy chains if you aren’t careful. We know. Several of us here at Electrek have done it.
The FREY EX Pro not only features high-end parts like a RockShox Lyric fork and Magura MT5e hydraulic brakes, but it even comes with dual batteries so you can ride farther and stay on the trails longer.
I’ve personally taken this e-bike back UP a downhill mountain bike course – that’s how powerful it is.
It may be expensive, but it saves you several thousand dollars compared to many European electric mountain bikes with similar components but a fraction of the power in the FREY.
See my full review of the FREY EX Pro here.
- Motor: 1 kW continuous, 1.5 kW peak-rated Bafang Ultra mid-drive motor
- Top speed (tested): 59 km/h (36 mph)
- Battery: Dual 48V 14Ah packs (1,344 Wh total)
- Range: Varies considerably by ride style/terrain, but 30-100 km (20-60 miles) is the ballpark
- Weight: 34 kg (75 lb)
- Price: $5,580
Tern GSD
The Tern GSD improves upon the Tern HSD with even more capability and even nicer components. There are multiple versions that can take you up to nearly $10k, but even the lower-tier versions are not “low tier,” if you know what I mean.
Parts like automatically engaging electric locks, 10-speed Shimano Deore transmissions, Magura MT5e quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, and more set these e-bikes apart from the rest of the pack.
If you’re getting a Tern GSD, you’re getting a fully qualified car replacement. There are many people who use these instead of buying a second car. When you look at it like that, the price suddenly seems pretty reasonable.
Check out our full review of the Tern GSD here.
- Motor: Bosch Cargo Line mid-drive
- Top speed: 32 km/h (20 mph) with electric assist
- Range: 42-85 km (26-53 mi) depending on pedal input
- Battery: Bosch PowerPack 400 Wh
- Weight: 33.6 kg (74 lb)
- Price: $5,399

title: Qcells to introduce U.S. domestic frames for residential solar panel lineup - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The manufacturer partnered with Aluko Group to supply U.S.-made aluminum frames from Tennessee, aimed at streamlining domestic content bonus qualification under increasing IRA thresholds.
Ryan Kennedy
17 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Manufacturing
pv magazine USA Week
Qcells announced plans to launch new versions of its residential solar panel series featuring U.S.-made aluminum frames by the end of 2026.
The updated residential product offerings, which include the company’s Q.Tron AC and Q.Peak Duo AC lines, will incorporate aluminum frames extruded, anodized, and fabricated at supplier Aluko Group’s integrated facility in Halls, Tennessee. The initiative is aimed at helping residential installers and third-party ownership TPO providers qualify for the Investment Tax Credit ITC domestic content bonus adder.
Under the Treasury Department’s domestic content guidance, solar hardware must meet specific domestic manufacturing thresholds to qualify for the 10% tax credit bonus. Qcells noted that keeping all three core stages of frame manufacturing, including extrusion, anodization, and fabrication, within the United States provides greater clarity for installers and financing partners when evaluating compliance.
The domestic frame offering comes as the statutory domestic content threshold for clean energy projects begins stepping up toward 55% for projects commencing construction in 2027.
“Through this partnership to produce modules with domestic frames, we are furthering our commitment to U.S. manufacturing, supporting clean, affordable energy and giving our customers the certainty they need to qualify projects for the domestic content bonus,” said Il Hyeong No, head of Qcells North America’s residential business.
Supply chain localized in Tennessee
Aluko Group’s manufacturing plant in Lauderdale County, Tennessee, is expected to reach full commercial production by the end of 2026. Once operational, the plant will have a planned annual capacity to manufacture enough frames to support 4 GW of solar modules.
Aluko plans to invest more than $107 million into the facility over five years, creating 285 full-time jobs. The company operates what it describes as the only facility in the U.S. performing all three major frame production steps under one roof.
“By carrying out extrusion, anodizing, and fabrication here in the United States, we are delivering a product that offers transparency and confidence at every step of the process,” said Jinwoo Park, president of Aluko Group.
The move expands Qcells’ broader domestic manufacturing push across its vertically integrated operations in Dalton and Cartersville, Georgia, where the company operates large-scale module and component assembly operations.
Want to learn more about the scaling of U.S. solar supply chains and domestic content rules?
Join us for
pv magazine USA Week
to attend the session Scaling Solar Production in the U.S. This panel addresses the real-world execution of policy-driven announcements, scaling domestic production, and navigating complex domestic content thresholds.
The session will feature Qcells Global Chief Technology Officer Danielle W. Merfeld alongside fellow expert panelists Finlay Colville, Founder of Terawatt PV Research; Jim Wood, CEO of SEG Solar; and Zennia Villanueva, Vice President of Quality at RETC, part of the VDE Group.

today to reserve your spot.
