title: Brazil’s new curtailment rules unlikely to revive utility-scale solar investment - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Brazil’s new curtailment rules offer greater regulatory certainty for solar developers, but uncertainty over future generation cuts and financial risks continues to weigh on investment. Industry experts expect new utility-scale solar projects to remain limited despite progress on compensation and curtailment allocation.
Lívia Neves
17 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
A utility-scale PV project in Brazil
Large-scale solar developers in Brazil have received two updates on past and future generation curtailment. Curtailment rates of around 25%, combined with uncertainty over compensation, have frequently been cited as reasons for developers to surrender project authorizations. While the new curtailment rules offer greater certainty and predictability, a recovery in investment will depend on other factors.
In 2026 alone, developers surrendered authorizations for 923 solar projects in Brazil, representing more than 40.6 GW of capacity and BRL 134 billion ($26.3 billion) in lost investment, according to a study by the Brazilian Solar Photovoltaic Energy Association (ABsolar). The association said the figures show that curtailment, along with the lack of clear criteria for classifying curtailed energy and determining compensation, has become a decisive factor in investment decisions, even in regions with little history of curtailment.
The pace of authorization cancellations has accelerated since 2025, shrinking the pipeline of projects available for future capacity expansion. Data from Brazilian electricity regulator Aneel show that 2,492 power plants, with a combined potential capacity of 110 GW, held authorizations in January 2026. That figure has since fallen to 60 GW.
Solar generation curtailment reached an average of 1.4 GW in 2026, equivalent to 25.3% of total solar generation during the period. The volume of curtailed electricity is already approaching the total recorded for the whole of 2025.
Compensation and curtailment rules
The risk of curtailment and uncertainty over compensation have brought investment in new utility-scale solar projects to a standstill. In July, Brazil’s Ministry of Mines and Energy issued Ordinance 140, establishing compensation rules for curtailment between Sept. 1, 2023, and Nov. 25, 2025. A total of 682 solar power plants, with approximately 25.5 GW of installed capacity, are eligible for compensation.
According to ABsolar, the main question is whether the compensation will be sufficient to allow companies to resume investment, meet financing obligations and restore their financial positions. “If the agreement is signed, companies will drop any ongoing legal actions in which they are seeking compensation for these curtailments, regardless of how the curtailments are classified,” the association said.
Absolar noted that the compensation proposal excludes curtailment caused by electricity oversupply, which already accounts for most curtailment events. Nevertheless, the ordinance offers some predictability over potential compensation. “With this proposal in hand, companies can engage in financial planning and, crucially, negotiate the restructuring of project-related debt with their banks,” the association said.
Meanwhile, Aneel published the outcome of Public Consultation 45 last week, formalized through Normative Resolution 1,170 on Oct. 6. The resolution establishes how future curtailment will be allocated among different generation technologies. The long-awaited clarification is expected to provide greater predictability for new investment in the sector.
Resumption of investment depends on other factors
Although the outcome of Public Consultation 45 (CP 45) provides greater clarity on how energy-related curtailment will be allocated and reduces regulatory uncertainty, the new rules alone are unlikely to trigger a significant wave of new greenfield wind and solar projects, Eduardo Tobias, founding partner of Watt Capital, told
pv magazine Brasil
However, the introduction of a curtailment priority order, which includes run-of-river hydropower plants and prioritizes higher-cost generation sources, is expected to reduce the share of energy-related curtailment allocated to wind and solar plants.
“Now that the allocation rules are clear, we still need to estimate the volume of energy-related curtailment in the future. In other words, we know how the ‘pie’ will be divided, but it remains difficult to estimate how big the ‘pie’ will be,” Tobias said.
That calculation depends on several factors, including growth in electricity supply, energy storage deployment, demand-response measures, electricity demand growth, gross domestic product (GDP) growth and electrification. The interaction of these variables makes it difficult to forecast how much curtailment individual projects will face over the long term.
Beyond estimating curtailment volumes, developers also face challenges in forecasting the Settlement Price for Differences (PLD), which determines the financial impact of curtailment on generators’ revenue. Because the price is not determined through bidding and its calculation rules change frequently, the combination of uncertain curtailment volumes and PLD fluctuations makes project risk assessments even more complex.
Against this backdrop, Tobias expects new greenfield wind and solar projects to remain the exception rather than the rule for an extended period.
“I see some room for new solar projects located close to electricity demand, with or without batteries,” Tobias said. “When generation is located close to demand, consumers avoid curtailment, transmission system usage charges (TUST), losses up to the system’s reference point and the allocation of capacity reserve charges (ERCAP).”
More curtailment on the horizon
Brazil’s National Electric System Operator (ONS) is also developing plans to introduce controls for distributed generation. As distributed generation (DG) continues to expand, industry representatives are calling for economic and regulatory incentives to make some small-scale distributed generation resources dispatchable.
One proposal involves encouraging consumers to invest in battery storage systems to absorb surplus generation and reduce the need for curtailment.
To help establish the necessary procedures, Absolar is preparing a study on the conditions for implementing distribution system operators (DSOs) and managing distributed generation. The study will focus on technical requirements, governance and transparency.
The association argues that these decisions should not be left solely to distribution utilities. Instead, it advocates the involvement of independent entities in managing distributed generation to improve economic efficiency.

title: Beyond recruitment: What really keeps women in solar - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
This week, Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) shares insights from its contribution to SolarPower Europe’s EU Solar Jobs Report 2026, exploring what attracts women to Solar+ and what makes them stay, progress or leave. Drawing on a survey across its network in 22 European countries, WiSEu highlights a clear message: purpose brings women into the industry, but their everyday experience of leadership, opportunity and workplace culture shapes whether they build their careers within it.
Women in Solar+ Europe
17 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Europe’s solar and storage industry has just reached a milestone worth celebrating: close to one million jobs in 2025, according to SolarPower Europe’s
EU Solar Jobs Report 2026
. But headline employment figures tell us how many people the sector employs. They say very little about who stays, who progresses, and who quietly walks away.
That is why Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) chose to look beyond representation in its contribution to this year’s report. Our article,
Beyond representation: what actually keeps women in Solar+
, draws on a survey of women across our network in 22 European countries. Instead of asking how many women work in solar, we asked a harder question: why do they come, why do they stay, and what pushes them out?
The mission opens the door
Our findings confirm something many of us already feel. Women are drawn to solar above all by its purpose, the chance to contribute to climate action and the energy transition. At the recruitment stage, the industry’s pull is clearly working.
But purpose alone does not keep people. Once inside, what matters shifts towards everyday workplace experience: career growth, genuine flexibility, a stable organisation, fair pay and an inclusive culture. Our conclusion is simple: women join Solar+ for the mission. They stay, or leave, for the employer.
“Nobody I know came into solar specifically for the perks. We came because we wanted to evolve the energy system. But purpose doesn’t replace a manager who backs you. At some point, the employer has to deliver.” says Carmen Madrid
Founder of WiSEu.
A retention risk the industry can’t ignore
That shift matters, because retention is far from guaranteed. Nearly four in ten respondents say they are likely to look for a new role within the next year. At a time when the report expects overall solar employment to contract towards 2030 while shortages persist in critical roles, losing experienced, committed people is a cost the sector cannot afford.
¨Renewable energy is a sector that inspires people to join, but inspiration alone is not enough to keep them. To build a resilient and diverse workforce, organisations must create environments where people can grow their careers, see role models they can relate to, and feel genuinely supported by strong and inclusive leadership,¨ says
Zoraida Bejarano
, Head of Talent at NextEnergy Group.
Heard today, less sure about tomorrow
There is genuine good news. Women in our Solar+ industries largely feel able to speak up, share ideas and challenge senior colleagues. The problem lies further up the ladder. Confidence drops when it comes to understanding how to progress, having equal access to opportunities, and seeing women like themselves in senior leadership. Respondents also described a “motherhood penalty”: good policies on paper, undermined by cultures that slow the careers of those who use them.
¨It is essential for companies not only to update their policies on paper, but also to put them into practice by accommodating situations that require flexibility, such as parental leave or adjustable working hours, and ensuring that everyone has equal opportunities for career development and professional growth,¨ says
Maria Sabella,
Founder and CEO at Enlight Energy Services.
Leadership is the lever
When Women in Solar+ Europe asked women in our industries which single change would make the biggest difference, the answer was clear. Nearly half of respondents pointed to leadership: better management, more women visible in senior roles, and access to mentorship and sponsorship. Not more recruitment campaigns, better leadership of the people already there.
“Visibility matters, but role models alone won’t close the gap. Women need promotion criteria that are transparent, development plans that are followed through, and succession processes that are objective and evidence-led, and don’t depend on who happens to be in the room. When advancement is designed deliberately rather than left to chance, talented people – whatever their gender – do not wonder whether there is a path for them; they can see it,” adds
Joanna Thorpe
, Head of People and Talent at Sonnedix
“I believe strong leadership starts with recognizing potential in people, sometimes even before they recognize it themselves. Mentorship is important, but real progress comes when leaders turn encouragement into action through trust, responsibility and genuine opportunities to grow. For women in the solar and energy storage industry, having leaders who open doors, value different perspectives and empower talent can make all the difference,” says Aga Michalak, Head of Marketing and ESG Europe at Jinko.
Our view: solar has a “what happens next” problem
WiSEu’s message is that this industry doesn’t have a recruitment problem. It has a “what happens next” problem. Companies that want to hold on to the talent they worked hard to attract need to treat retention and progression as deliberately as hiring:
Track who stays and who advances, not only who joins.
Design flexibility around outcomes, not presence.
Invest in leadership quality, mentoring and sponsorship.
Make senior career paths visible and attainable.
This is not only a gender question; it is a competitiveness question. The report itself calls for inclusive, high-quality pathways into solar careers, and for measuring retention and progression rather than enrolment alone. Women in the sector have already committed to the energy transition. The question is whether the industry will commit to them in return.
Read the full findings
This article only scratches the surface. The complete Women in Solar+ Europe analysis, with detailed results on why women join and stay, how they experience voice and progression at work, and the levers they would prioritise, is published as Box 2 of SolarPower Europe’s
EU Solar Jobs Report 2026
Download the report from SolarPower Europe here
and read “Beyond representation: what actually keeps women in Solar+”.
Whether you lead a team, shape HR policy or are building your own career in Solar+, we invite you to read the data, share it with your leadership, and join the Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) so we can keep shaping the leadership intelligence our industries need.

title: France to ease grid connection rules for solar-plus-storage projects up to 25 MW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
France plans to ease grid connection rules for solar-plus-storage projects with installed capacity of up to 25 MW, provided grid injection does not exceed 17 MW. The measure is part of a broader government initiative to accelerate electrification and improve electricity demand flexibility.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
17 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Following an initial package of measures announced in April, French government spokesperson Maud Bregeon has unveiled additional initiatives aimed at accelerating the electrification of the economy and improving electricity demand flexibility.
The government identified significant untapped potential in the residential sector, particularly through smart management of heating, domestic hot water and electric vehicle (EV) charging. It estimates that these measures could reduce associated energy costs by up to 35%.
To unlock this potential, the government plans to make subsidies for heat pumps conditional on smart-control capabilities from 2027. Households installing such systems could save between €150 ($168.8) and €200 annually.
For EV charging infrastructure, the government intends to work with industry stakeholders to ensure that smart-control functions are enabled by default in new installations. Options under consideration include connecting charging stations to Linky, France’s nationwide smart electricity metering system, or introducing connectivity solutions that automatically schedule charging during off-peak hours. These measures could save households between €70 and €100 per year.
The government also plans to introduce flexibility requirements for industrial energy metering systems.
Smart meters and battery storage
The plan calls for greater use of Linky smart meters to manage household electricity consumption. Although the meters already support applications such as automated domestic hot water heating, many of their capabilities remain underused. The government intends to encourage their integration with residential energy management systems to improve demand flexibility.
Another measure targets grid connections for solar photovoltaic installations combined with battery energy storage systems. By the end of 2026, the government plans to allow projects with installed capacity of up to 25 MW to benefit from an exemption from the current 17 MW connection limit, provided their maximum power injection into the grid does not exceed 17 MW.
The measure is intended to facilitate grid connections for hybrid renewable energy projects, particularly solar-plus-storage installations, without increasing their maximum permitted grid injection.
France’s energy regulator, the Commission de Régulation de l’Énergie (CRE), has also outlined plans to encourage electricity consumption during periods of high solar generation.
New electricity supply products are being tested for potential commercialization through EDF Obligation d’Achat (EDF OA), the division of state-owned utility EDF responsible for purchasing electricity under France’s renewable energy support schemes.
The products would reflect the typical daily solar generation profile, with output peaking around midday before declining in the late afternoon. The aim is to encourage electricity suppliers to offer tariffs that incentivize consumers to shift demand to periods of abundant, lower-cost solar generation.
Industry targets for 2030
Several French energy companies and industry associations have also announced commitments to expand electricity demand flexibility by 2030.
Gimelec, a French trade association representing electrical equipment, automation and digital energy technology companies, aims to mobilize 6 GW of flexibility in commercial and service-sector buildings. It plans to support the installation of energy control and management systems in 50% of existing facilities.
EDF aims to introduce remote-control systems for energy-intensive equipment in five million customer households by 2030, targeting heating, domestic hot water, heat pumps and EV charging. The utility plans to use its EDF & Moi customer app to connect and manage these devices, positioning the platform as a household energy management tool.
French independent power producer Neoen has committed to deploying 1 GW of flexibility capacity by 2030.
Meanwhile, French energy storage and flexibility provider NW Group plans to invest €1 billion by 2030 to add 1.5 GW of capacity to its electricity flexibility platform in France. The company also intends to open the platform to industrial and residential consumers seeking to generate revenue from flexible electricity consumption.
Octopus Energy France has pledged to manage 1.5 million connected devices by 2030, representing an estimated 5 GW to 6 GW of flexible capacity.
The company expects the initiative to deliver €100 million in financial benefits to households and support the deployment of 15,000 remotely controllable heat pumps. It could also underpin a €150 million investment in a heat pump manufacturing facility, subject to the targeted deployment volumes being achieved.

title: Six-year testing highlights impact of reduced maintenance on PV plant operation during COVID-19 pandemic - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A six-year study of a 12 MW solar plant in Algeria found an average performance ratio of 82.6%, with annual electricity generation ranging from 19.83 to 21.41 GWh. Performance declined significantly in 2020 due to COVID-19-related maintenance restrictions, highlighting the importance of regular cleaning and upkeep.
Emiliano Bellini
17 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Utility-scale
The 12 MW solar plant in Sidi Bel Abbes
Researchers at Djillali Liabes University of Sidi Bel-Abbes have published the findings of a six-year performance assessment of a 12 MW grid-connected solar power plant in Sidi Bel-Abbes, western Algeria, covering the period from 2018 to 2023.
The study revealed a significant decline in the plant’s performance in 2020, primarily attributed to reduced maintenance activities amid restrictions imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“This drop in yield underscores the crucial role of regular maintenance in minimizing energy losses and sustaining optimal system performance,” the researchers said.
The solar plant in Sidi Bel Abbes uses Sunny Central 800CP XT inverters from German manufacturer SMA and 47,808 polycrystalline silicon HSL60-PB-1–250 modules from Hanwha Qcells, each rated at 250 W and mounted at a 34° tilt facing south. The installation is divided into six 2 MW subfields, each equipped with two inverters and connected to a step-up transformer.
The Sidi Bel Abbes solar plant was equipped with a monitoring system that records operational and meteorological data every 15 minutes in accordance with IEC 61724 standards. Its control room houses two computers, one for plant supervision and data collection and another for grid monitoring. An on-site weather station measures solar irradiance, ambient temperature, humidity and wind speed.
To minimize dust-related energy losses, the facility used a semi-automatic cleaning system featuring rotating brushes mounted on a tractor-towed frame. The researchers assessed the plant’s performance using several indicators, including reference yield, array yield, final yield, performance ratio and capacity utilization factor. They also evaluated inverter and overall system efficiencies to determine how effectively solar energy was converted into electricity.
Array capture losses and system losses were calculated to identify inefficiencies in electricity generation and conversion. Finally, the researchers examined long-term module degradation by tracking changes in effective peak power under standardized irradiance and temperature conditions.
The testing showed that ambient temperatures followed stable seasonal patterns, ranging from around 8–10 C in winter to 22–24 C in summer. Solar irradiation varied between 100 and 275 kWh/m² per month, with the highest levels recorded in June and July. Annual electricity generation ranged from 19.83 to 21.41 GWh, with 2019 recording the highest output, followed by 2023. Monthly production peaked at 2,258 MWh in August 2019, while the lowest output of 1,125 MWh occurred in January 2020.
Average daily reference, array and final yields were 5.65, 4.92 and 4.65 hours, respectively. Capture losses ranged from 0.3 to 1.5 hours per day, while system losses varied between 0.1 and 0.5 hours per day. Despite favorable irradiation conditions, the plant experienced a marked performance decline in 2020, attributed primarily to reduced cleaning and maintenance during COVID-19 restrictions. The performance ratio fell to 78.74% in 2020 from 85.37% in 2019, before gradually recovering to 84.83% in 2023. Its six-year average performance ratio reached 82.6%, exceeding that of several comparable installations worldwide.
Module efficiency generally ranged between 12% and 14%, while inverter efficiency remained stable at approximately 97–98%. The average annual capacity factor was 19.3%, reaching a maximum of 20.30% in 2019. The researchers also estimated degradation rates of 4.12% and 4.38% under two different irradiance and temperature conditions. They concluded that the plant demonstrated competitive long-term performance despite temporary operational setbacks, highlighting the importance of regular maintenance and improved cleaning systems for sustaining electricity production.
Their findings were presented in “
Evaluation of an Algerian solar power plant efficiency: Six-year performance of 12 MWp grid-connected photovoltaic
,” published in the
Journal of Engineering Research

title: Spanish researchers test low-height agrivoltaics in vineyards - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Spanish researchers have tested low-height agrivoltaic systems at three vineyards, demonstrating electricity generation with negligible impacts on grape production. The systems achieved land equivalent ratios of 1.16 to 1.53, highlighting their potential to improve land-use efficiency.
Lior Kahana
17 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
A research team in Spain has experimentally investigated the integration of low-height photovoltaic systems into vineyards.
They explained that low-height agrivoltaic systems could offer several advantages over conventional elevated installations, particularly in vineyards where maintaining existing cultivation practices is essential. By positioning PV modules closer to the ground and integrating them between vine rows, these systems can reduce structural material requirements, installation costs and visual impact. They could also minimize interference with vineyard machinery and routine agricultural operations while limiting shading during critical stages of grape development.
The researchers installed and tested three agrivoltaic systems at commercial vineyards in southeastern Spain, assessing their agricultural performance during the 2024 harvest season and monitoring electricity generation over 14 months.
“This study presents the first field-scale validation of the vertical agrivoltaic design proposed by our group,” the researchers said. “The systems were designed with the primary aim of preserving the agronomic integrity of the vineyard, avoiding critical shading during sensitive periods, and maintaining the operational routines of viticulture. Energy production was considered secondary and constrained by agronomic and structural design.”
The researchers conducted the study at three commercial vineyards in southeastern Spain. At Bodegas San Isidro, they installed a 2.34 kW vertical bifacial PV system in rows oriented at −63°, using monocrystalline silicon modules measuring 0.6 m × 1.1 m. At Bodegas Carchelo, they deployed Venetian blind-style monofacial configurations with a combined capacity of 1.56 kWp in rows oriented at −8°, using modules measuring 0.3 m × 1.1 m. At Bodegas Evine, they installed a 2.4 kW vertical monofacial system in rows oriented at +8°, using modules measuring 0.6 m × 1.1 m.
During the 2024 harvest, the scientists compared grape performance in areas influenced by the PV modules with that of control areas without modules. For each replicate, they randomly selected 350 berries and assessed grape yield, sugar concentration, titratable acidity, pH, total anthocyanin content and total polyphenol index.
The team also monitored electricity generation at the inverter level over 14 months. It estimated annual electricity production per hectare and assessed land-use efficiency using the land equivalent ratio (LER), taking an optimized ground-mounted PV system as the reference.
“We demonstrate that meaningful energy production can be achieved under a cultivation-first design logic, resulting in LER consistently above unity with 1.16–1.53, thus confirming real land-use efficiency gains,” the researchers said.
They also identified opportunities to increase PV installation density in low-trained vineyards, potentially achieving capacities comparable to conventional ground-mounted PV systems without requiring additional land or interfering with agricultural activities. Under this scenario, the LER could reach 1.95.
The vertical bifacial system at Bodegas San Isidro achieved the highest estimated annual electricity production, at 555,905 kWh/ha, followed by the vertical monofacial system at Bodegas Evine, at 383,764 kWh/ha, and the Venetian blind-style system at Bodegas Carchelo, at 304,716 kWh/ha.
The researchers also proposed a structural design requiring between 141 kg and 161 kg of steel per kWp of installed capacity while maintaining adequate mechanical performance. They said the figures were at the lower end of reported steel requirements for agrivoltaic installations.
The findings are presented in the study “
Low-height vertical photovoltaic integration in vineyards with negligible agronomic impact
,” published in
Renewable Energy Focus
. The research team included scientists from Spain’s
Polytechnic University of Cartagena
Murcian Institute for Agricultural and Environmental Research and Development (Imida)

title: Dutch regulator flags EU cyber gap for cloud-controlled home batteries - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A Dutch regulator says EU cybersecurity rules should target companies by how much power they can control remotely, not by their size, and wants home energy devices certified independently under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA).
Brian Publicover
17 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Residential
The Netherlands’ digital infrastructure inspectorate, the Rijksinspectie Digitale Infrastructuur, says a faulty update or cyberattack on manufacturer and aggregator platforms could switch enough inverters, home batteries, heat pumps and EV chargers at once to destabilize the grid. It argues in a recently published position paper that the EU Cyber Resilience Act and NIS2 directive only partly cover the companies behind those platforms.
The biggest risk sits not in individual devices but in the backend systems of manufacturers, energy management system providers and aggregators, and in the cloud platforms they use, according to the inspectorate. Because large groups of devices connect to the same backend, a single point of entry can control many of them.
A sudden imbalance between supply and demand of 3 GW or more can disrupt the grid, the regulator says, citing research by SolarPower Europe. It says the number of heat pumps and EV chargers in the Netherlands grew fivefold between 2019 and 2024.
The inspectorate identifies three ways large numbers of devices could be affected simultaneously. A manufacturer or other party with remote access could push a faulty update or setting, attackers could exploit vulnerabilities in devices or their control platforms, or a state could compel manufacturers and service providers under its jurisdiction to cooperate.
Under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, such devices face only general cybersecurity requirements and manufacturers assess their own compliance, while the requirements apply only to products placed on the EU market from Dec. 11, 2027.
NIS2 applies mainly according to company size rather than the capacity a company can control remotely, so smaller companies fall outside unless designated by national authorities, as do energy companies and manufacturers without an EU establishment.
The provisional list of entities under the Network Code on Cybersecurity, whose obligations take effect in mid-2028, does not yet include manufacturers or energy management system providers.
The inspectorate proposes three remedies. It suggests device-specific harmonized EU standards and adding categories of these devices to the CRA’s list of important class II products, which would require an independent assessment before they could be sold in the European Union.
It also proposes bringing companies that can remotely control enough capacity to endanger grid stability under NIS2, regardless of their size or location, and strengthening the grid’s digital autonomy by limiting dependence on companies outside the European Union that can influence devices at scale.
Isabel van der Leij, the inspectorate’s manager of digital resilience for the energy sector, said the devices make the electricity system smarter and more sustainable but introduce new risks that require both secure devices and resilience across the energy system as a whole.
A European Commission expert group recommended in a report this month that solar inverters be classified as important class II products under the CRA,
alongside restrictions on high-risk suppliers
. The group said its analysis did not cover EV chargers, heat pumps or battery storage systems, which it could assess later.
At a cybersecurity forum in Brussels on Oct. 8, researchers from the European Network for Cyber Security (ENCS) showed how a compromised smart-home device could be used to send commands to a residential inverter or home battery on the same network.
“More high-power IoT devices are being deployed every day, and vulnerabilities in some of these devices have already been exploited and could be exploited again to disrupt the electricity grid,” said Harm van den Brink, a security researcher at ENCS. “In the short term, we need independent security testing, prioritized according to the amount of power potentially affected, combined with vulnerability management by manufacturers.”
The inspectorate presented its paper at the ONE Conference in The Hague, where researchers from Modat and the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre also reported
8,547 internet-facing systems at European solar and wind sites
that should not be reachable online.

title: Large-scale solar projects in Australia reach record 3.5 GW of annual investment decisions - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The latest Clean Energy Regulator data shows investment in solar is setting a new annual record with solar final investment decisions for the September 2026 quarter at 1 GW, adding to 3.5 GW already achieved in 2026.
Ev Foley
17 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Highlights
The latest Clean Energy Regulator (CER) data shows investment in solar is setting a new annual record with final investment decisions (FID) for the September quarter sitting at 1 GW, following 2 GW in Q2, adding to the year’s already tallied 3.5 GW, and is approximately 30% above the previous annual solar FID record.
2.1 GW of total large-scale renewable capacity reached FID in the September quarter, which is an equal highest quarterly result, and brings total renewable FID to October 2026 to 5 GW.
That is higher than the previous full-year record of 4.9 GW and brings large-scale FID totals to almost 17 GW since 2022.
This figure shows the capacity of large-scale wind and solar power stations approved by the CER to generate large-scale generation certificates over time. |
Image: Clean Energy Regulator
Rooftop solar added 90,042 installations and 894 MW of capacity in the September quarter, which is 35% higher than in Q3 2025, and year-to-date rooftop solar capacity is 45% higher than at the same point in October 2025.
Rooftop solar installations in Q3 were 39% higher than Q3 2025, and has so far added 2.8 GW in 2026, which almost matches the whole of 2025, with three months to go.
Q2 2026 was the biggest rooftop solar capacity quarter on record at 1 GW, and over 13 GW of small-scale solar has been installed since 2022.
This figure shows the installed capacity in megawatts (MW) and the number of small-scale rooftop solar installations over time.
Approved capacity under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program (CHBP) reached 15.3 GWh by the end of September, up 1.9 GWh in Q3, and up from less than 2 GWh at the same time in 2025, with total home battery capacity in Australia now more than 5 times greater than when the scheme began on 1 July 2025.
Cheaper Home Batteries approved capacity has more than tripled during 2026, growing from 5 GWh at the end of 2025 to 15.3 GWh at the end of Q3. With total home battery capacity, including that installed before the scheme, around 19 GWh, it is more than 5 times greater than when the scheme began.
New South Wales (NSW) has 5.6 GWh of approved home battery capacity, followed by Victoria and Queensland at about 3.2 GWh each.
The data shows about half of approved battery installations are retrofits to existing solar, while about half are going in with new or upgraded rooftop solar.
This figure shows the cumulative installed capacity of approved small-scale battery installations by state and territory and installation date following the commencement of the Cheaper Home Batteries Program on 1 July 2025. |
Image: Clean Energy Regulator
Federal Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen said more renewable energy reaching final investment decision is “what progress looks like”.
“Renewable investment has already broken the annual record with three months still to go. And it isn’t just investment; last month renewable energy generated more electricity in the national grid than fossil fuels,” Bowen said.
“Investors, as well as Australian households and small businesses, are backing Australian renewable energy because they see a government with a clear policy that is working and we’ll continue to get on with the job.”

title: In a first, an F-22 Pilot commands a combat drone from the cockpit
content: A US Air Force F-22 Raptor pilot directed an uncrewed YFQ-44A Fury aircraft in flight for the first time, marking a major step toward a future in which crewed fighters command autonomous drones during combat missions.The demonstration, conducted earlier in October 2026, paired the stealth fighter with Anduril’s Fury Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA). Instead of flying the drone remotely with individual controls, the F-22 pilot sent high-level tactical instructions that the drone’s onboard autonomy software interpreted and executed.The test advances the Air Force’s effort to turn uncrewed aircraft into autonomous wingmen that can accompany crewed fighters, extend their reach, and provide additional combat capacity without requiring a pilot in every aircraft.An airborne quarterback directs the droneAccording to The War Zone, the F-22 and YFQ-44A took off from Edwards Air Force Base in California and joined up in the air. The pilot then transmitted an updated mission plan to the drone through a tactical data link.The Air Force described the human pilot as an airborne “quarterback,” issuing tactical directives while the Fury’s onboard software handled their execution. The demonstration included dynamic flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks.The pilot was not manually controlling every movement of the uncrewed aircraft. Instead, the test showed how a human could direct a semi-autonomous platform while its software handled the details of executing instructions.The Air Force and Anduril did not disclose the full cockpit configuration used during the demonstration. Previous work on drone-control interfaces has explored tablet-like displays and supporting hardware that allow pilots to communicate mission instructions without significantly disrupting their primary flying duties.The longer-term goal is to let a single fighter pilot direct multiple collaborative combat aircraft, though managing several autonomous wingmen will require further software development, testing, and operational procedures.What is the YFQ-44A Fury?The Fury is Anduril’s entry in the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program, which aims to develop uncrewed aircraft that can operate alongside conventional fighters.The aircraft is being developed as a lower-cost complement to crewed combat jets. Depending on the final configuration and mission, future CCAs could carry sensors, electronic warfare equipment, or weapons, helping distribute tasks across a larger force.The Air Force has selected both Anduril’s YFQ-44A and General Atomics’ YFQ-42A for the first increment of the program. The service is pursuing both designs as it develops the technology, tactics, and support systems required to field autonomous aircraft.The Fury has already demonstrated other capabilities. In July 2026, the Air Force announced that a YFQ-44A had launched an AIM-120 air-to-air missile during a live-fire test against a digital target. That test validated another step in integrating the aircraft with weapon systems, but it was separate from the recent F-22 control demonstration.A step toward crewed-uncrewed combat teamsThe F-22 test is part of a much larger initiative to integrate autonomous aircraft into future air combat. The Air Force wants CCAs to increase the number of aircraft available for a mission while giving pilots additional sensing, targeting, and engagement options.The service is also working through practical challenges, including how drones will be deployed and maintained, how pilots will manage their workload, and how commanders can trust autonomous aircraft to behave predictably in complex environments.This demo shows that a fighter pilot can issue tactical instructions to a purpose-built CCA in flight, providing a foundation for further testing. The next challenge is to turn that capability into a reliable operational system, potentially allowing crewed fighters to direct multiple uncrewed aircraft as part of a coordinated combat formation.

title: Doomsday glacier may keep melting even if oceans cool, studies find
content: Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier, nicknamed the “Doomsday Glacier,” may keep losing ice for generations even if the ocean waters melting it cool dramatically. New research also suggests its contribution to sea-level rise by 2100 could be roughly twice as large as some models previously estimated.The findings highlight two related challenges. Past changes have pushed the glacier into a retreat that may be difficult to reverse, while new modeling suggests scientists may have underestimated how warm seawater reaches beneath it.Why Thwaites Glacier mattersLocated in West Antarctica, Thwaites is one of the region’s largest contributors to ice loss. Its complete collapse could eventually raise global sea levels by an estimated 65 centimeters (about 26 inches), although that is a long-term risk rather than a forecast for this century.The glacier’s vulnerability lies partly in the way it meets the ocean. Much of its ice rests on bedrock below sea level, while its floating ice shelves help regulate how quickly ice flows toward the sea.Relatively warm ocean water can melt the underside of these floating shelves. As the shelves thin, they provide less resistance to the ice behind them, allowing the glacier to retreat inland and contribute more water to the ocean.A study published in Nature Communications on October 12, 2026, examined how seawater penetrates the broad transition zone where grounded ice begins floating. The researchers found that representing this zone as several kilometers wide, rather than as a narrow boundary, helped their model reproduce the observed retreat and thinning from 1996 to 2023.Under a constant-climate scenario, the model projected up to 30 millimeters (1.2 inches) of global sea-level rise from Thwaites by 2100, about twice the average of earlier projections used for comparison. The study also found that the glacier could detach from a stabilizing underwater ridge as early as 2038 in some simulations.Why cooling the ocean may not be enoughA separate study led by the British Antarctic Survey, published in Geophysical Research Letters, explored a stark hypothetical scenario: what if ocean-driven melting beneath the ice shelves stopped entirely?Researchers ran three independent ice-sheet models over 150 years. In the simulations, neighboring Pine Island Glacier began thickening and advancing, but Thwaites continued losing ice throughout the period, albeit at a declining rate.The result suggests that Thwaites is still responding to past environmental changes. Its retreat has altered the glacier’s geometry and relationship with the seafloor, meaning that simply reducing ocean melting may not restore its earlier state on century-long timescales.Importantly, the zero-melting scenario is an extreme modeling experiment, not a realistic prediction. The study does not establish that every future change is irreversible or that Thwaites must accelerate toward total collapse.Can we stop the Doomsday Glacier from melting?There is no proven technology that can restore Thwaites Glacier to its historical condition. The latest findings instead point to two priorities. Reducing the warming that drives ocean melting and preparing for sea-level rise that may now be difficult to avoid.Cutting greenhouse gas emissions remains important because continued ocean warming could intensify ice loss beyond the changes already set in motion. The British Antarctic Survey researchers emphasize that future losses could be exacerbated if emissions are not reduced.Scientists have also explored more direct interventions, including seabed curtains intended to restrict warm water from reaching vulnerable ice shelves and other proposals to stabilize glaciers. For coastal communities, the implications extend beyond Antarctica. Sea-level rise increases the risk of flooding, erosion, and storm-surge damage, making adaptation planning increasingly important even if emissions fall.The Doomsday Glacier is not a countdown to a single catastrophic event. It is a warning that changes to Earth’s largest ice sheets can continue long after the conditions that triggered them begin to improve. Scientists may not be able to reverse all the ice loss already set in motion, but limiting further warming can still influence how much more ice is lost, and how much the seas ultimately rise.

title: China unveils automated interception drones to neutralize aerial threats
content: China showcased low-cost, AI-guided drone interceptors at a counterterrorism forum in Beijing this week, where experts discussed new technologies and their potential misuse by terrorist groups.The high-speed interceptors were showcased at the Great Wall-2026 International Forum on Counterterrorism, which ran from 13 to 15 October. Organized by the People’s Armed Police, the event brought together more than 320 defense experts and military delegates from 62 countries.Discussions focused on the growing role of AI and uncrewed systems in counterterrorism, as well as the risks they pose for recruitment, reconnaissance, and coordinated attacks.AI-guided interceptors target small dronesThe interception drones featured AI guidance systems designed to neutralize “low, slow and small” unmanned aerial vehicles with high precision and rapid response times.Their low-cost design was a feature of the display, although the supplied report did not disclose prices, speeds, engagement ranges, or details about how the drones destroy their targets.The exhibition also included humanoid robots, robotic dogs, unmanned ground vehicles, drone detection equipment and laser-based defense systems. Together, the systems covered reconnaissance, swarm defense and control, and precision response capabilities.According to state broadcaster CCTV, the display showed AI’s expanding role across counterterrorism operations, from situational awareness and incident response to assessments after an operation.The People’s Armed Police, which organized the forum, is China’s paramilitary force responsible for internal security, riot control and counterterrorism.Autonomous systems create new security risksExperts at the forum warned that terrorist organizations were increasingly exploiting autonomous drones, drone swarms, encrypted communications and AI.These technologies could support radicalization, recruitment and fundraising while helping groups conduct complex attacks across multiple domains.Science and Technology Daily reported that AI and unmanned technologies were expanding the reach and methods of terrorist attacks, while groups continued shifting the geographical focus of their operations.The report also described UAVs with greater autonomy, stronger cyberattack capabilities, and increased use of drone swarms. Improved resilience to electronic warfare could further complicate efforts to disrupt these systems.The discussions highlighted how technologies developed to improve security could also become tools for groups seeking to evade existing defenses.Experts call for safeguards against misuseRegulating autonomous intelligence systems emerged as a central challenge, covering who develops, sells, purchases, and deploys them, as well as how they are eventually disposed of.“Terrorists might exploit AI models for learning and training, for which the developers must configure their large language models to prevent misuse,” Wu Mingxi, an expert in military intelligence and systems, told CCTV.Wu added that generative AI could help malicious actors produce deepfake videos and misinformation, creating further challenges for authorities.“If we do not pay attention to the application of AI technology and fail to prevent its misuse by terrorist organizations and violent extremists, the consequences will be disastrous,” said Peng Jijun, secretary general of the forum’s organizing committee.The forum’s discussions underscored the need for coordinated international regulation as autonomous systems become more capable and accessible.

title: Deep brain hub prepares for sights and touch before they arrive: Study
content: Scientists have discovered that a tiny midbrain structure anticipates visual and physical sensations before they occur, aligning with the idea that the brain does not simply wait for sensory input, but predicts what is about to happen.A new study from MIT and Northeastern University, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggests that brain regions that process sensory information also help prepare for these incoming stimuli.The superior colliculus, which researchers described to Medical Xpress as “one of the most well-studied brainstem structures,” shows distinct activity patterns before people see an image or feel physical pressure.Researchers continued to explain that the project grew out of a known idea in neuroscience called predictive processing. The brain does not simply wait around for input; it constantly predicts and prepares, if only because “reacting after the fact is costly,” the researchers explained.Brain scans reveal predictive activityThe researchers examined 80 adults using ultra-high-field 7-Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Using this technology, they observed activity in the superior colliculus at a resolution of approximately 1 millimeter.Half of the participants viewed images. The other half received mechanical pressure on their left thumbs. Researchers told Medical Xpress that two questions drove these methods: “We wanted to answer two questions. First, is the human superior colliculus organized the way animal studies suggest, with vision concentrated in its upper layers and touch in its deeper layers? Second, how does it respond before a sensory stimulus arrives, when that stimulus is expected?”Before stimulation, these participants performed a shape-based decision-making task. The researchers then compared the changes that occurred between the two states of activity. Visual stimuli produced more activity in the superficial layers of the superior colliculus. Touch drove more activity in the deeper layers.“More importantly, the same layer-specific pattern showed up even before the stimulus arrived, when people were only anticipating a picture or a touch,” according to Medical Xpress.The study noted that the nature of the anticipated sensory experience affected these activity patterns in the superior colliculus differently.Prediction extends beyond the cerebral cortexThe researchers used machine learning to determine whether brain activity patterns could distinguish between visual and tactile experiences. They observed similar patterns during anticipation and actual stimulation, corroborating the findings from the initial brain scans.The researchers also detected these predictive responses in two sensory-processing regions of the thalamus, suggesting that anticipation involves multiple structures beneath the cerebral cortex.This study challenges conventional understanding in neuroscience. Typically, prediction is considered a “higher-level function that happens in the cortex,” according to Medical Xpress. However, the study suggests that deeper brain structures that relay information to the cortex are part of a broader network designed to prepare for incoming input.The researchers acknowledged limitations such as the absence of eye-movement recordings during scanning and uncertainty. Some of the observed activity might simply have been general anticipation related to the experiment itself.Nevertheless, the findings demonstrate that the superior colliculus participates in predictive processing rather than simply reacting to incoming information.“In sum, the present work demonstrates that subcortical nuclei are not passive recipients of sensory input but, rather, that they both react to and anticipate sensory input from the external world,” the researchers concluded in the study.

title: China pours record $583 billion in research as US weighs science cuts
content: China increased research and development spending by 8.2% in 2025, pushing total investment above $583 billion as Beijing expands support for basic science, universities and strategic technologies. The latest figures from China’s National Bureau of Statistics highlight a growing contrast with the US, where the Trump administration has proposed steep cuts to federal research budgets, including reductions of 39% for the National Institutes of Health and 55% for the National Science Foundation in its proposed 2026 budget.China’s spending remains second only to that of the US in absolute terms, but its sustained investment in scientific research and industrial development is strengthening its position in the competition over semiconductors, AI and other advanced technologies.Increased funding for basic science and universitiesChina’s total R&D expenditure exceeded $583 billion in 2025, and according to state news agency Xinhua, spending grew at an average annual rate of 10% over the five years through 2025, making China one of the fastest-growing major research investors, the South China Morning Post reported.Basic research recorded the largest percentage increase among the three main categories, rising 13.3% year over year to roughly $40 billion. Despite that growth, basic research still accounted for just over 7% of total R&D spending. Research expenditure at higher education institutions rose 11%, to approximately $48 billion.China’s overall research spending was 3.4 times Germany’s and 3.5 times Japan’s, according to the reported figures. Its R&D intensity, measured as expenditure relative to gross domestic product, reached 2.8% in 2025, surpassing the OECD average for the first time and placing the country 12th globally.Businesses remained the main source of research investment, with enterprise spending exceeding around $420 billion for the first time, accounting for more than 77% of the national total. Investment was concentrated in major industrial and technology centers, including Guangdong, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shandong provinces, as well as Beijing and Shanghai.US research budgets face proposed cutsChina’s investment growth comes as the Trump administration seeks to reduce federal support for scientific research. A Harvard Business School article cited in the report said the administration froze or terminated about $3 billion in National Institutes of Health grants in early 2025, affecting approximately 3,800 research projects.Uncertainty over federal funding has already placed pressure on institutions that depend on government grants to support researchers, laboratories, and long-term projects. Furthermore, Interruptions to funding can affect not only individual projects, but also the training and retention of researchers needed to maintain a country’s technological capabilities. Meanwhile, China’s government has signaled that it intends to direct further resources toward basic science and technologies considered important for economic competitiveness and national security. Chinese science and technology minister Yin Hejun has identified stronger fundamental research as a prerequisite for major technological breakthroughs, with Beijing seeking to address bottlenecks in sectors such as semiconductors, industrial machinery and high-end scientific instruments.

title: Nuclear reactor design uses swappable cores to beat salt degradation
content: Big tech firms in the US are pouring billions into advanced nuclear power to feed energy-hungry artificial intelligence. Across the Atlantic, European scientists are tackling the technology’s biggest engineering headache: corrosive liquid salt.Dutch startup Thorizon has teamed up with research institute TNO. Together, they have launched an experimental materials program. The goal is straightforward. They need to find metals that can survive inside molten salt reactors without failing. Early testing has already begun in Petten and Amsterdam.Increasing demand for molten salt reactorsMolten salt reactors run at near-atmospheric pressure and rely on passive safety mechanisms if power fails. They can also be configured to produce far less long-lived waste than conventional US commercial reactors. These traits make them attractive for data centres and heavy industry needing round-the-clock power.Yet their internal environment is hostile. Liquid fuel salts operate at intense heat, often topping 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit. Over time, this mixture corrodes structural metals while radiation weakens them from within.Thorizon plans to work around this problem rather than fight it indefinitely. Standard reactors rely on permanent vessels built to last half a century. Thorizon takes a modular route. It seals the liquid salt inside self-contained cartridges. Operators will simply pull out the old units and slot in fresh ones every five to ten years.“Our cartridge design makes material degradation a manageable engineering challenge,” said Kiki Lauwers, chief executive of Thorizon. She noted that the new trials will give regulators and operators hard data on cartridge lifespans.“This programme will provide the independent evidence needed to validate that design and give regulators and operators confidence in material performance and cartridge lifetime,” added Lauwers.Running stress trialsSafety agencies require strict experimental proof before licensing advanced reactor designs. TNO will run stress trials, simulate corrosion rates, and track failure points to show how these alloys hold up over time.“These innovations can only move from concept to deployment on the basis of strong scientific evidence,” remarked Tjark Tjin-A-Tsoi, chief executive of TNO.The findings will support safety licensing for Thorizon’s PIONEER test reactor in Petten. Later, they will underpin Thorizon One, the company’s planned commercial model.The two Dutch groups are expanding the work across borders. They are bringing in partners such as Delft University of Technology, NRG PALLAS, the French atomic agency CEA, and the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre.Need for steady baseload energyThe initiative arrives as power grids face unprecedented demand. In both North America and Europe, clean electrification and digital infrastructure are outstripping renewable additions like wind and solar. Modern grids still require steady baseload energy that runs day and night.To help close that gap, the Netherlands aims to build 7 gigawatts of nuclear capacity by 2050. Small modular reactors are central to that plan. Officials want compact plants that hook directly into factories and server farms.If the Petten trials succeed, Thorizon’s swappable core could offer a clear path forward. Proving the materials work may finally turn molten salt from a lab promise into a commercial reality.

title: Heat pumps cut heating costs by 44% compared to coal in poultry farms
content: Researchers from Sakarya University and ETA4 Engineering in Turkey have tested an air-source heat pump (ASHP) heating system designed for commercial poultry houses. This, they found, can not only save money on heating, but can also precisely control the environmental conditions necessary for raising chickens commercially at scale.In fact, according to the researchers, using heat pumps can save around 44% in costs compared to comparable coal-fired heating. “The annual cost comparison showed a reduction from $15,506.26 for coal heating to $8,692.48 for the heat pump system, corresponding to approximately 44% lower annual heating costs,” study author Zekeriya Parlak told PV Magazine in an interview. “The comparative analysis also indicated that the heat pump offered additional cost savings of approximately 18% relative to coal, 42% relative to natural gas, 48% relative to fuel oil, and 65% relative to direct electric resistance heating under the evaluated conditions,” he added.At present, most poultry houses use a combination of coal-, gas-, or oil-fired boilers to circulate heated air throughout them. While very effective, this can be a very costly enterprise, especially in colder weather. The team, however, wondered if a heat pump could be a viable alternative. Heat pumps for happier chickensIn case you are unaware, these work a bit like a refrigerator in reverse. Rather than generating heat by burning fuel, it extracts thermal energy from outside air, even when that air is cold, and transfers it indoors. The secret power of this setup is something called the coefficient of performance (COP). A conventional electric resistance heater converts approximately one unit of electricity into one unit of heat. A heat pump, on the other hand, can deliver several units of heat for every unit of electricity it consumes because it’s moving existing thermal energy rather than generating all the heat from electricity. While performance varies with outdoor temperatures, heat pumps can deliver substantially more useful heat per unit of energy purchased than conventional electric resistance heating.With the team’s new system, the heat pump heats water and uses a large tank to buffer the heat. From here, heated water is circulated to fan coil units (FCUs) to circulate warm air throughout the poultry house.To test their hypothesis, the team set up their system in one of three identical chicken houses at the same commercial chicken farm in Sakarya. Two of the buildings kept their conventional boiler setup, while the third had the new heat pump and FCU system installed.During testing, the team measured and monitored energy consumption, but also checked that warmth was evenly distributed throughout each test building. This matters because young broiler chickens (chickens raised for meat) require very warm conditions to mature.More efficient and cheaperCold spots in buildings tend to cause young chickens to cluster together for warmth, which can impact growth and welfare. So, to ensure optimum conditions for the chickens, the team employed computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software to model how warm air moved through the building.Using this, they ran various models for FCU setup and found that seven units strategically placed within each 296-foot (90.3-meter) long, 49-foot (15-meter) wide chicken house offered the best temperature and airflow distribution. Each of these houses had a floor space of around 14,585 square feet (1,355 square meters) and contained around 21,000 chickens.“The main novelty of this research lies in its integrated experimental, numerical, and techno-economic evaluation of an ASHP as a direct replacement for conventional coal-fired heating in commercial broiler houses,” research lead Zekeriya Parlak told PV Magazine in an interview. “This work combines real-world energy consumption measurements from three identical broiler houses on the same farm, analytical heat-demand calculations, experimentally validated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, and comparative heating-cost assessments,” he added.Looking ahead, the team plans to integrate solar panels, batteries, and heat recovery systems to further improve efficiency. You can view the study for yourself in the journal Case Studies in Thermal Engineering.

title: 5,200-ton nuclear attack submarine built to hunt enemy warships unveiled
content: France has just rolled out its fifth next-generation nuclear attack submarine (SSN), ready for final fitting-out and testing. Called the Rubis (S639), the boat is the latest in a planned fleet of six Suffren-class submarines.These boats are intended to replace the French Navy’s existing Rubis-class SSNs, which have been in service since the 1980s. This replacement programme hopes to see all six new SSNs done and dusted by 2030.Designed and built by the French shipbuilder Naval Group, the 326-foot (99-meter) long Rubis left its construction hall on October 16, 2026, in Cherbourg. This means the submarine’s main structure is effectively now complete.The boat now requires finishing touches like integrating and testing onboard systems, final work on propulsion, and installation of electrical and combat systems. Following this work, the Rubis will begin sea trials, likely sometime in 2027, though no official date has been publicly announced.5 out of 6 SuffrensIf the Rubis passes those trials, she will officially be ready for official acceptance by the French Navy, likely in late 2027. The sixth and final boat, the Casabianca (S640), will join its sisters sometime over the next few years.The new Suffren-class (developed under the Barracuda programme) is a substantial upgrade over the Rubis-class and will enable the French Navy to maintain its attack submarine capability well into the middle of the century. Key features include its X-shaped rear rudder and control setup and pump-jet propulsion system.The latter offers the class significant noise-reduction capabilities, increasing its underwater stealth capabilities. SSNs like these are designed for conventional combat, but can also be used in intelligence gathering roles and fleet protection. Such submarines can be used to hunt and kill enemy submarines, and also attack surface ships unseen.They also come with land strike capabilities and can be used for other specialist missions like covert operations. This can include missions like delivering combat divers into contested regions. Its nuclear reactor gives it enormous endurance without needing to surface or snorkel to operate diesel engines. That said, things like food supplies, crew requirements, and maintenance are generally more limiting than fuel.Futureproofing the navy“It is with great pride and a deep sense of responsibility that we today transferred the Rubis, the fifth Suffren-class nuclear attack submarine, to its launch platform. This crucial milestone comes just 17 months after that of the nuclear attack submarine De Grasse, a symbol of our commitment to our customers,” said Pierre Éric Pommellet, Chairman and CEO of Naval Group.“In an extremely challenging operational environment, manufacturers must rise to the occasion to deliver to sailors the ships they need to carry out their missions. This event is also an opportunity to recognize the integrated teamwork with the DGA, our partners, and the crew—the foundation of our collective success,” he added.Looking ahead, the French Navy plans to upgrade the Suffren-class over its lifespan rather than allow them to become obsolete through its “Evol SNA.” This will allow them to modernize them as and when needed. There are also plans afoot by the French defense procurement agency (DGA) called SNA3G, which are preliminary plans for an eventual replacement of the Suffren-class in the future. It is understood that this is not yet an official programme.

title: Record-breaking X-rays squeezed into spot 100,000x smaller than a hair
content: Electrons move so quickly inside atoms and molecules that studying their behavior requires flashes of light lasting just a fraction of a billionth of a billionth of a second. Now, scientists have found a way to concentrate these ultrashort X-ray flashes into a tiny spot, making them more powerful at the point where they hit a sample. In an experiment at the European X-ray Free-Electron Laser (European XFEL), researchers achieved record intensity and fluence for hard-X-ray attosecond pulses. Their peak intensity exceeded 1020 watts per square centimeter.“This is a world record in intensity and fluence for a hard-X-ray attosecond pulse,” Ichiro Inoue, lead researcher and a scientist at the University of Tokyo, said. This advancement could help scientists investigate how electrons respond to intense light and, eventually, explore ways to control them during chemical reactions.How precision mirrors pack X-ray energyThe experiment, conducted in April 2026, used X-ray flashes lasting an estimated 300 attoseconds. An attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second, making these pulses useful for investigating some of the fastest processes involving electrons.The researchers directed the pulses through an advanced Kirkpatrick–Baez (AKB) optical system consisting of two precision mirrors. Each flash reflected off the mirrors four times in total. One mirror focused the X-rays vertically, while the other focused them horizontally, concentrating the beam into a spot measuring just 180 × 330 nanometers. In short, the researchers somehow focused the X-rays into an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross-section of a typical human hair.The achievement builds on earlier work at the European XFEL, where researchers demonstrated hard-X-ray attosecond pulses at terawatt-scale power. However, generating powerful pulses is only part of the problem. The energy must also reach the sample in a sufficiently concentrated form to produce the desired effects, a challenge also faced by other X-ray laser technologies used to study matter at tiny scales.“A few years ago, we demonstrated terawatt-scale hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL. But generating powerful pulses is only the first step. For experiments, what really matters is what we can deliver to the sample. With this advance, we can now use attosecond X-rays to explore highly nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter,” Jiawei Yan, one of the researchers, said.Copper atoms help verify the record intensityTo check the intensity independently, the team directed the X-ray pulses onto a copper foil and examined the light emitted by its atoms.The incoming X-rays knocked electrons out of deep inner shells of copper atoms, leaving vacancies, or holes. Electrons from outer shells then fell into those vacancies, releasing energy as X-rays.Under sufficiently intense illumination, this emission can stimulate other excited copper atoms to release X-rays traveling in the same direction. The resulting amplification produces a stronger, more concentrated signal. This process is called amplified spontaneous emission (ASE), a phenomenon related to the emission processes that make X-ray lasers possible.“It is almost magical to see this happening. Normal fluorescence goes in all directions, regardless of the direction of the incoming beam. But when the ASE threshold is crossed, you see the light cone starting to condense into the forward direction,” said Anders Madsen, who wasn’t directly involved in the study but is the project leader of the facility where the experiment was conducted.Initially, the ASE signal grew rapidly as the researchers increased the pulse energy. At higher energies, however, the signal began to level off, a behavior known as saturation. This response was consistent with the extremely high intensities estimated from the pulse energy, duration and focused spot size, providing an independent check on the calculations.The next step in capturing electrons in action The achievement could help researchers study how electrons behave in atoms and molecules, including how matter responds to intense X-ray illumination. In the longer term, these studies could contribute to efforts to control electrons during chemical reactions. Researchers are already exploring ways to capture such rapid changes, including experiments imaging electrons and atoms during chemical reactions. However, the experiment demonstrated the production and verification of intense X-ray pulses, not direct control of electrons during a reaction.For now, the researchers used an AKB mirror system brought from Japan. European XFEL expects to receive its own system in early 2027. Once installed and tested, it is intended to make these short, intense X-ray flashes available to researchers worldwide using the facility’s MID instrument. The study is published in the journal Optica.

title: New flying taxi to feature 30G crash seats, Northrop navigation
content: UK-based Vertical Aerospace has selected a 30G energy-absorbing seating system and Northrop Grumman navigation technology for its Valo electric flying taxi, as the company moves toward aircraft certification and production.The Bristol-based aircraft developer announced two long-term supplier agreements on October 16. South Korea’s ANH Structure will develop and manufacture the aircraft’s seats, while Germany-based Northrop Grumman LITEF will supply its LCR-110 inertial reference system.The seating system will incorporate technology designed to absorb high impact forces during a crash. Meanwhile, the navigation system will provide essential flight information, including the aircraft’s orientation, heading and position.Both systems are intended for Valo, Vertical’s piloted electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, which is being developed to carry four passengers. The agreements establish supplier responsibilities but do not mean the completed systems have been certified for the aircraft.Seats designed for impactANH Structure will design, develop, certify and manufacture a common seating platform for Valo’s pilots, observers and passengers. The seats will incorporate the company’s proprietary 30G energy-absorption technology.The 30G figure refers to acceleration equivalent to 30 times Earth’s gravity. Energy-absorbing seats are designed to manage forces transmitted to occupants during an impact, potentially reducing injury risks.However, Vertical has not disclosed crash-test results for the finished Valo seating system. The supplier will still need to complete development, testing and certification before the seats enter production.ANH holds European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) design and production organization approvals. These credentials allow the company to undertake approved aerospace design and manufacturing work, although they do not constitute certification of the new seats.The agreement covers the process from detailed design through industrial production. A common seating architecture could also help Vertical use similar components across different versions of its aircraft.Navigation supports flight controlNorthrop Grumman LITEF, a German subsidiary of the US defense and aerospace company, will supply the LCR-110 inertial reference system.The system provides information about an aircraft’s attitude, heading and position to flight-critical systems. Attitude describes how an aircraft is tilted or oriented in flight, while heading indicates the direction it is pointing.Such information is important for an eVTOL aircraft, which must manage vertical takeoffs, transitions between flight conditions, and conventional forward flight.According to Vertical, the LCR-110 meets applicable EASA and Federal Aviation Administration technical standards for inertial reference equipment. Its existing approvals do not remove the need to integrate and certify the system as part of Valo.The agreements add to Vertical’s supplier network, which includes Honeywell Aerospace, Sonaca, Evolito and Hyundai WIA.Vertical plans to use a common aircraft platform for four- and six-passenger configurations, as well as electric, hybrid-electric and autonomous variants. These remain part of its development strategy rather than a range of certified aircraft.The company says it has approximately 1,500 preorders from customers across four continents, including American Airlines, Avolon and Japan Airlines. Those commitments do not represent completed aircraft deliveries.The latest agreements secure suppliers for two important aircraft systems, but Vertical must still complete development, integration, and regulatory certification before Valo can enter commercial service.

title: 14,000-ton nuclear submarine fires missiles, hit target 745-mile away
content: One of Russia’s nuclear-powered submarines of the Russian Pacific Fleet has fired has fired Oniks and Kalibr cruise missiles. The weapons were launched from Novosibirsk, a Project 885M Yasen-M class multi-purpose nuclear-powered submarine.Reports revealed that Kalibr successfully hit its designated target from 745 miles away. While Oniks cruise missile engaged a maritime target, and covered a distance of 105 miles.Submarine’s combat capabilities testedThe launches demonstrated the submarine’s ability to engage targets at sea and on land while operating underwater in the Pacific Ocean. The launches formed part of scheduled military training activities aimed at testing the submarine’s combat capabilities.The two launches highlighted the submarine’s ability to employ different missile systems against distinct types of targets, combining maritime strike capabilities with long-range attacks against land-based objectives.Russian Pacific Fleet vessels secured the exercise area, which was closed to civilian shipping and aircraft during the missile launches.The Novosibirsk belongs to Russia’s Project 885M Yasen-M class of multipurpose nuclear-powered submarines. These vessels are designed to perform a range of missions, including engaging surface ships and attacking land-based targets with cruise missiles.Submarine is first serial-production vessel of Project 885M classThe submarine is the first serial-production vessel of the Project 885M class, according to TASS. Its keel was laid on July 26, 2013, and it was launched on December 25, 2019.On September 28, 2022, the submarine arrived at its permanent base in the Kamchatka region, joining Russia’s Pacific Fleet alongside the Knyaz Oleg, a Project 955A Borei-A-class strategic nuclear-powered submarine.The Yasen-M program represents an important component of Russia’s modern naval force, providing multipurpose submarines capable of conducting operations across different maritime environments. The Oniks and Kalibr missile families are among the principal weapons associated with Russia’s Yasen and Yasen-M-class submarines. The Oniks is an anti-ship cruise missile designed to engage surface vessels. Its use during the exercise simulated an attack against an opposing naval force.The Kalibr family includes cruise missiles designed for different missions, including strikes against land-based targets. During the reported exercise, the missile was used against a designated target at the Kura testing ground.The successful launches, as reported by the Russian Defense Ministry, demonstrate the operational use of both missile systems during a single training activity. However, the ministry’s statement does not provide independent verification of the results or disclose additional technical details about the missiles’ performance.The reported missile exercise involving the Novosibirsk highlights Russia’s continued emphasis on submarine-based strike capabilities in the Pacific region. By firing Oniks and Kalibr cruise missiles at maritime and coastal targets, the submarine demonstrated the operational use of two key weapons systems associated with the Yasen-M class.While the Russian Defense Ministry reported that both missiles hit their designated targets, the broader significance of the exercise lies in its demonstration of the submarine’s multipurpose role and its contribution to Russia’s Pacific Fleet.
