title: Anthropic's confidential bill limits federal power to halt models
content: Anthropic wants Congress to set strict limits on when federal authorities can stop advanced AI models from reaching users. A confidential draft bill obtained by POLITICO would tie government intervention to specific catastrophic threats and require judicial approval for suspensions.The proposal would give frontier AI developers a clearer legal framework while restricting the circumstances that could trigger government action. It also raises questions about how much oversight regulators should exercise over increasingly capable systems.Strict thresholds for interventionUnder the proposal, federal authorities could seek to halt a model only when it presents a foreseeable, imminent threat. Qualifying risks must involve more than $1 billion in damages or the deaths or serious injuries of over 50 people.The bill limits those threats to three scenarios. These include creating or releasing biological weapons, models escaping their developers’ controls, or cyberattacks. Other forms of harm would fall outside this specific intervention framework.Anthropic says the legislation reflects its Advanced AI Framework, which it has promoted among federal and state lawmakers since June. “These are sensible policies we believe Congress should act on,” an Anthropic spokesperson reportedly said.Independent evaluators would oversee compliance. They would register with the Commerce Department and periodically assess frontier AI developers and their models. Evaluators could receive payment from the companies they inspect, provided their compensation does not depend on their findings.If an assessment identifies an imminent threat covered by the bill, evaluators must notify Commerce within 72 hours of completing their review.Courts would control suspensionsThe proposal would prevent the Commerce Department from independently shutting down a model. Instead, the department would need to seek an order from a federal judge in the District Court for the District of Columbia.The draft also bars other federal departments, agencies, and officials from suspending a model’s development, deployment, or internal use. That restriction could reduce the risk of sudden executive action against AI developers.The issue has particular relevance following US export controls that reportedly sidelined two advanced Anthropic models over the summer. The episode raised concerns across the technology industry about government officials restricting access to powerful systems.However, the bill would also preempt certain state requirements covering public risk disclosures, independent evaluations, and critical incident reporting. That provision could reignite disputes over whether Washington should establish a national standard or preserve stronger state protections.Congress weighs competing proposalsAnthropic’s draft enters a crowded legislative debate over how the United States should regulate frontier AI. Representatives Lori Trahan and Jay Obernolte have advanced the FRONTIER Act, which would authorize government intervention against risky models and override some state laws.In the Senate, Majority Leader John Thune has worked with Senators Amy Klobuchar and Ted Cruz on legislation targeting catastrophic AI risks. However, some safety advocates and Senator Maria Cantwell want a stronger federal review process.Other lawmakers have pushed for more sweeping restrictions. Representative Greg Casar and Senator Bernie Sanders have called for pausing advanced AI development and banning superintelligence.Anthropic’s proposal takes a narrower approach. It would require frontier developers to establish safety frameworks, publish transparency reports for new models, protect whistleblowers, and report critical incidents to Commerce.Whether lawmakers accept those limits will help determine how much authority the federal government gains over advanced AI systems. The debate also centers on whether a single national framework can protect the public without giving regulators excessive discretion.

title: Tiny optical chip uses two lasers to generate precise signals for future atomic clocks
content: Researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have demonstrated a chip-based optical frequency comb that uses two lasers to generate precise light signals without the bulky stabilization equipment required by some earlier designs.The development could help make optical atomic clocks smaller and more suitable for use outside laboratories. Such clocks could eventually support navigation systems in drones, submarines and other vehicles when GPS signals are unavailable or jammed.The device relies on a tiny ring-shaped structure called a microresonator. Light from two lasers circulates through the ring, producing a series of evenly spaced optical frequencies that can be used as highly precise measurement references.The researchers, working with colleagues at the Joint Quantum Institute (JQI), a partnership between NIST and the University of Maryland, say the approach addresses a key obstacle in developing compact frequency combs: generating stable, high-quality signals without additional power-hungry equipment.Two lasers replace hardwareOptical frequency combs work much like rulers for light. Instead of measuring distance with evenly spaced marks, they produce a series of precisely separated frequencies that allow scientists to measure light with exceptional accuracy.These devices are important components of optical atomic clocks, which use the vibrations of atoms at optical frequencies to measure time.Conventional optical frequency comb systems can require multiple components to stabilize their signals. Although researchers have already developed miniature versions using microresonators, maintaining the required signal quality can still demand additional equipment.NIST’s approach sends light from two lasers into the same microresonator. Their interaction generates the evenly spaced frequencies needed for optical measurements while avoiding the extra stabilization hardware associated with earlier single-laser methods.The researchers fabricated chips containing as many as 300 tiny ring-shaped resonators. These structures provide the optical environment needed to generate the comb signals.According to NIST, the two-laser technique produces high-quality frequency combs without relying on the bulky laboratory setup that has limited some previous designs.The demonstration concerns the frequency-comb component rather than a complete portable atomic clock. NIST has not reported a finished navigation system using the new device.Precision timing beyond GPSOptical atomic clocks could provide accurate timing references for navigation systems that cannot depend entirely on satellite signals.GPS works by using precisely timed signals from satellites to determine location. When those signals are blocked, disrupted or deliberately jammed, vehicles may need other methods to maintain reliable navigation.Compact optical clocks could eventually contribute to such systems by providing stable timing references onboard vehicles, reducing dependence on external signals.Potential applications include autonomous drones, submarines and other vehicles operating in environments where satellite navigation is unreliable. NIST also identifies mineral exploration and oil and gas surveying as possible uses for portable optical clocks.However, the research does not establish that the new microcomb can independently provide GPS-free navigation. Additional clock components and navigation technologies would be required.The next challenge is translating the demonstrated optical performance into practical instruments that meet the size, power and reliability requirements of mobile platforms.By reducing the supporting hardware needed to produce stable optical frequencies, the researchers have demonstrated one component that could help make precision timing equipment more portable.

title: US Navy turns 164,000-pound Hercules into nuclear command aircraft
content: The U.S. Navy’s next airborne nuclear communications aircraft has reached its first major milestone, but extensive engineering work remains before it can enter service. A C-130J-30 Super Hercules arrived at Lockheed Martin’s Marietta, Georgia, facility on October 15 for conversion into the E-130J Phoenix II.The aircraft will eventually replace the Navy’s E-6B Mercury fleet, which relays strategic instructions between national command authorities and U.S. nuclear forces. Its arrival begins the process of turning a military transport into a specialized communications platform designed for one of America’s most critical defense missions.Heavyweight starting pointThe C-130J-30 provides a substantial airframe for the Navy’s requirements. Lockheed Martin lists its maximum takeoff weight at 164,000 pounds, with a standard maximum payload of 46,700 pounds. Its operating empty weight stands at approximately 88,252 pounds.Range varies with the aircraft’s load. The manufacturer lists approximately 2,485 miles with a 40,000-pound payload. Four turboprop engines power the aircraft, giving it the performance needed for demanding military transport operations.However, carrying mission equipment presents different engineering challenges than transporting conventional cargo. The Navy needs an aircraft capable of supporting specialized communications hardware during extended operations. Integrators must adapt the existing platform to accommodate those requirements.The C-130J family offers an established military airframe and modern avionics. Its existing capabilities provide a starting point for the conversion, although the transport configuration cannot perform the new mission without substantial modifications.Engineering the Phoenix IINorthrop Grumman will integrate the specialized equipment that transforms the C-130J-30 into the E-130J Phoenix II. Planned work includes communications systems and enhancements intended to improve survivability during operations.The aircraft’s primary responsibility will involve the Navy’s Take Charge and Move Out (TACAMO) mission. These aircraft maintain communication links between national leadership and nuclear forces, including ballistic missile submarines.That role demands reliable equipment capable of transmitting strategic instructions during severe national security crises. Engineers must integrate the necessary systems into the aircraft while ensuring they support the mission’s operational requirements.U.S. Navy Capt. Roger Davis, who manages the airborne strategic command and communications program, described the delivery as an important milestone. He emphasized the airframe’s suitability for integrating the systems required by the mission.The delivery does not mean the aircraft can begin operational service immediately. Integration and subsequent testing must establish whether the modified platform meets the Navy’s requirements.Return to HerculesThe Phoenix II program also reconnects the Navy’s strategic communications mission with the Hercules family. The service previously operated the EC-130Q for TACAMO duties from 1963 through 1993, according to Lockheed Martin.That earlier aircraft established a historical precedent for using the Hercules platform in this specialized role. The E-130J brings the concept back with a newer airframe and updated mission equipment.The Navy must now complete the conversion before the aircraft can assume its intended responsibilities. Its progress will depend on integrating the communications hardware and demonstrating the system’s performance through testing.Replacing the E-6B Mercury fleet will require more than a new aircraft. The Phoenix II must deliver dependable strategic communications capabilities, making the conversion and validation phases central to the program’s success.

title: Blue Origin eyes weekly launches for its 400-foot New Glenn rocket
content: Blue Origin is expanding its Florida operations to support a much faster launch schedule, targeting multiple New Glenn flights per week by the end of the decade. The plan includes a $330 million manufacturing expansion, additional launch pads, and new facilities for payload processing and booster refurbishment.The company says it has invested more than $3 billion in Florida infrastructure. Its operations now span more than 20 sites across Brevard and Orange counties, supported by over 5,000 employees and 500 suppliers.The expansion aims to address a central challenge in commercial spaceflight: increasing launch frequency requires more than additional rockets. Manufacturers must produce hardware faster, ground crews must prepare missions in parallel, and reusable boosters must return to service efficiently.Scaling new Glenn productionBlue Origin is expanding Rocket Park, its 1.37-million-square-foot manufacturing campus near NASA’s Kennedy Space Center. A $330 million project will add capacity for producing New Glenn’s 9×4 second stage.Scheduled for completion in summer 2027, the expansion will support annual production of up to 150 upper stages. That output would provide substantial manufacturing capacity as the company pursues a higher flight rate.The factory is also gaining automated machining, welding, material handling, and inspection systems. These technologies can improve production consistency and help workers identify defects earlier.Additional investments in chemical processing, fairing preparation, tooling, and storage will support the movement of hardware through the manufacturing process. Blue Origin also aims to produce nearly all its components and systems in-house, while maintaining support from external suppliers.Preparing multiple missionsManufacturing more rocket hardware will not increase launch frequency unless teams can prepare several missions simultaneously.Blue Origin is developing a customer integration facility with the U.S. Space Force at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. The complex will feature four payload bays, two encapsulation bays, and a dedicated area for processing multiple payloads together.Launch infrastructure is also expanding. Blue Origin is restoring LC-36A following an anomaly earlier this year, while LC-36B will become the operational base for New Glenn 9×4.It will accommodate New Glenn’s 7×2 and 9×4 configurations, including national security missions. A separate vertical integration facility under construction will support the 9×4 vehicle and enable parallel vehicle and payload preparations.The company has also requested permission to increase LC-36’s annual launch limit from 12 to 50 flights. Additional launch pads are planned for the Space Coast, using construction methods demonstrated at LC-36B.Reusing boosters more efficientlyNew Glenn’s reusable first stage requires a recovery network capable of supporting repeated flights. Port Canaveral currently hosts Jacklyn, the rocket’s sea-based landing platform, while Blue Origin develops two additional platforms.The new vertical integration facility will also process recovered boosters. Teams will inspect returning stages and prepare them for refurbishment before subsequent missions.Beyond rocket production, Blue Origin operates facilities across Cocoa, Melbourne, Orlando, and Titusville. These locations support fabrication, thermal protection systems, tooling, logistics, and materials handling.Its Lunar Permanence program also relies on facilities across Florida to manufacture, integrate, and test hardware. The company’s Club for the Future nonprofit has reached nearly 700,000 Florida students and 65,000 educators since 2019.Blue Origin’s expansion reflects the infrastructure demands of a higher launch cadence. Manufacturing capacity, parallel mission preparation, and faster booster turnaround will determine how effectively the company can translate its ambitions into more frequent flights.

title: Meet the spacetech CEO who's betting everything on nuclear micropower
content: In our latest episode of Lexicon, we sat down with Peter Cabauy, CEO and founder of City Labs, to explore why power, rather than propulsion, could become the defining technology of the next era of space exploration.Cabauy explains how the Moon’s extreme environment, particularly its 14-day-long nights and brutally cold temperatures, presents a major challenge for long-term lunar operations, and why nuclear micropower could be the key to keeping rovers, equipment, and future lunar outposts running.Also, subscribe to IE+ for premium insights and exclusive content!Trickle, not a flood“The moon is a very inhospitable environment,” Cabauy told us. “Your rover is only going to last 14 days because that’s the length of the lunar day,” he added.After that comes the lunar night, another 14 Earth days of darkness where temperatures plunge to levels colder than liquid nitrogen. “We’ve all seen what happens when you drop a flower inside liquid nitrogen and hit it with a hammer,” he said. “Imagine trying to make a rover survive in that type of environment,” he added.That, he explained, is where nuclear micropower comes in. Unlike conventional nuclear reactors, City Labs develops microscopic power sources that generate electricity and heat through the natural decay of tritium.“The easiest visual is a solar cell,” Cabauy said. “Instead of receiving light, we receive beta radiation.”Those electrons generate a tiny but continuous electrical current. While the output is measured in nanowatts or microwatts rather than kilowatts, the systems never need recharging and continue operating for decades.“The real power is that it’s continuous,” he said. “It works under extreme temperatures.” He was quick to stress that these devices were never intended to replace lithium batteries.“If you can use a lithium battery for what you need to do, please do it,” he said. “This is for what you can’t possibly replace.” Instead, they are designed for environments where replacing a battery is impossible, prohibitively expensive, or life-threatening.A pacemaker was one example. “Do you really want to do extra operations?” he said.Powering the lunar economyCabauy believes reliable long-duration power would become one of the key enabling technologies behind a permanent human presence on the Moon. “Nuclear micropower is what’s going to enable that lunar economy,” he said.Rather than relying on miles of copper cable or solar panels that become useless during the lunar night, he envisages thousands, or even millions, of autonomous sensors scattered across the lunar surface.“You can drop thousands and hundreds of thousands of these devices into permanently shadowed craters,” he said.Those sensors could provide navigation, communications, environmental monitoring, and scientific data while operating continuously in places where sunlight never reaches. “Think of millions of these tritium-powered small devices on the lunar surface,” he said. “This is where it’s going.”He also believes they could support future missions to Mars, heliocentric spacecraft and new generations of miniature satellites.“We’re excited about what we can’t think about today,” he said. “Other engineers are going to come up with those ideas.”From peanuts to tritiumGrowing up, one of his heroes was George Washington Carver, the scientist famous for finding hundreds of applications for peanuts. “George Washington Carver tried to find a thousand uses for peanuts,” Cabauy said. “At City Labs, we try to find a thousand uses for tritium.”That mindset, he explained, shaped everything the company he would eventually build now pursues. He explained that tritium is an ideal radioisotope because it was relatively benign, already had an established regulatory framework, and benefited from a reliable supply chain.“It wasn’t an accident that we chose tritium,” he said. Today, City Labs uses it for beta-voltaic batteries, heat sources, and future propulsion concepts.Engineering was only half the battleDespite spending two decades developing the technology, Cabauy argued the engineering challenge had only been part of the story. “The engineering was tough,” he said. “But I would advocate that regulatory is equally as tough.”Much of the company’s innovation focused not only on making the devices work, but making them safe enough to fit within existing regulatory frameworks. “We found ourselves engineering towards the regulatory as well as the commercial scale-up,” he said.That work ultimately led to what he described as a significant milestone.“We’re crossing the nuclear space threshold as the first to be able to commercially launch a nuclear device.”The year everything nearly endedPerhaps the most compelling part of the conversation had little to do with nuclear technology. Cabauy shared some candid information about the darkest period in the company’s history.“That was a bad year,” he said, recalling 2017 when City Labs came close to shutting down. “I told my wife, ‘I quit. I just can’t do this,” he said.The following morning brought a different realisation. “I said, ‘Well… I can’t quit. I just don’t know how.'”The company lacked the money even to decommission its facilities, leaving little choice but to keep turning up. What changed, he said, was his mindset.“When opportunities came, I just said yes.”Instead of analysing every decision as a physicist, he returned to the curiosity that had driven him as a child. “I decided to go back to the childhood inventor,” he told us.Unexpectedly, people began offering help. “I started realising there’s more than just paying people to work,” he said. “There’s also the vision of where we’re going.”That shift proved transformational. “People would offer me help,” he said. “All I had to do was say yes.”Soon afterwards, contracts began arriving from companies including Lockheed Martin Space and medical device manufacturers, setting City Labs on the path it follows today.Looking beyond spaceAlthough lunar exploration dominated much of the discussion, Cabauy believes that nuclear micropower would also find applications much closer to home. He highlighted downhole oil and gas monitoring, industrial sensors and next-generation medical implants.One area he found particularly exciting was leadless pacemakers. “If you want to reduce it down to the size of a grain of rice, nuclear is probably going to be it,” he said.He also pointed to research exploring tiny tritium-powered light sources designed to help prevent diabetic retinopathy, potentially slowing vision loss in patients.A commercial nuclear space ageLooking ahead, Cabauy remains focused on City Labs’ upcoming milestones, including the launch of its Bohr satellite demonstration mission. “We’re opening up this nuclear space age,” he said.Ultimately, however, his ambitions extended beyond City Labs itself.“I want City Labs to lead the way in terms of nuclear micropower,” he said. “But it’s not just us. It’s many others using this type of technology to find applications and use cases where our imagination isn’t enough today to know what they will be,” he told us.

title: Google speeds protein prediction 8.6-fold for targeted cancer drugs
content: Google researchers have developed a method that speeds up protein structure prediction by 8.6 times, potentially accelerating the discovery of molecules for targeted cancer therapies.The researchers used the approach to design proteins that bind tightly to fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP), a molecule associated with solid tumors. Such binders could eventually help researchers develop treatments that target cancer-associated tissue more precisely. The results were obtained through laboratory experiments after computationally designing candidate molecules.The work is part of three Google Research projects exploring how artificial intelligence agents can design biological molecules, analyze experimental results and work with laboratory equipment. The projects also demonstrated improvements in DNA molecule discovery and robotic experimentation.Google said the research aims to reduce the time and computational resources required to test biological designs. However, the systems remain experimental, and the protein binders have not been demonstrated as cancer treatments.Faster protein structure predictionsDesigning a protein that attaches to a specific biological target requires researchers to predict how the molecules fold and interact. This involves generating candidate protein structures, designing sequences, and checking whether the resulting molecules are likely to bind.The final prediction stage can consume substantial computing power, particularly when the target protein is large.Google researchers developed a technique called “surgical epitope excision,” which focuses structural predictions on the local region where a designed protein is expected to attach, rather than processing the entire target.According to Google, the approach accelerated structure prediction by 8.6 times without sacrificing structural accuracy in its tests.The researchers applied the method to FAP, using yeast surface display and fluorescence-activated cell sorting to screen engineered protein candidates. These techniques allow researchers to examine large numbers of protein variants and identify those that bind to a target.The strongest experimentally tested designs achieved single-digit nanomolar binding affinity, indicating a tight molecular interaction. In a separate computational comparison using equal computing resources, a scientist working with an agent achieved nearly twice the predicted hit rate of a scientist working alone.These findings concern early-stage molecular design. The researchers have not established whether the binders can safely or effectively treat cancer.Robots learn from experimentsA separate Google project tested whether agents could improve DNA aptamers, short molecules that fold into shapes capable of attaching to specific proteins.Researchers conducted three design-and-testing rounds targeting myoglobin and alpha-thrombin. Each round took seven to 10 days and involved synthesizing DNA candidates, testing their binding behavior and using sequencing results to guide subsequent designs.By the third round, confirmed on-target hit rates reached 33.5 percent for myoglobin and 42.1 percent for alpha-thrombin. The latter achieved 98.5 percent specificity.Google also introduced VERID, a digital laboratory model that tracks robotic equipment, liquid volumes, and experimental materials. It allows agents to simulate procedures and detect potential errors before sending commands to laboratory robots.In one dye-mixing experiment, an agent used repeated robotic tests and camera feedback to improve reconstruction accuracy more than fivefold.The three projects remain separate demonstrations. Google plans to combine its robotic control framework with molecular discovery workflows, with human oversight and biosecurity screening retained throughout the process.

title: Taiwan plans $4B Texas industrial park for Nvidia, TSMC suppliers
content: Taiwan plans to develop a $2 billion–$4 billion industrial park in Texas to strengthen semiconductor and artificial intelligence hardware supply chains linked to TSMC, Nvidia and other major technology companies, its Ministry of Economic Affairs said Friday.The proposed complex will be the first in a series of U.S. industrial parks designed to help smaller Taiwanese manufacturers establish operations in the country.The ministry said private businesses would provide funding while the government would offer financial and administrative assistance. The project will be developed in cooperation with the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association (TEEMA), which will help raise the necessary funding.Bringing suppliers closer togetherThe initiative aims to extend Taiwan’s overseas manufacturing expansion beyond major technology companies to the smaller businesses that supply them.The proposed parks would provide smaller Taiwanese suppliers with a base closer to major U.S. manufacturing operations, potentially easing logistical challenges and helping companies coordinate production with their customers.TSMC is a major manufacturer of advanced semiconductors, including chips used in Nvidia’s computing hardware, while Foxconn assembles AI servers and other electronic equipment.The government plans to support participating companies through loan guarantees and assistance with administrative requirements. It will also help coordinate discussions with U.S. federal and local authorities on matters including visas and land arrangements.According to Bloomberg, land has already been secured in Texas for the proposed industrial park. However, Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs has not confirmed the location and said that additional details would be provided later.More manufacturing sites consideredTexas is expected to be the starting point rather than the only location for the initiative.Foxconn Chairman Young Liu, who also chairs TEEMA’s Supervisory Committee, recently identified Arizona and Texas as potential locations for overseas science parks. Other locations under consideration include Mexico, Poland and India.Taiwanese electronics manufacturers have already been expanding their U.S. operations. TSMC has outlined a $165 billion investment plan in the country, while Foxconn and Wistron have expanded their manufacturing presence in Texas.The proposed industrial parks would build on that expansion by helping smaller suppliers establish facilities in the U.S. without having to navigate financing and administrative requirements entirely on their own.Taiwan’s announcement comes as other Asian economies expand their U.S. investment plans. South Korea has outlined a $350 billion investment framework covering sectors including manufacturing, energy and shipbuilding, while Japan has committed up to $550 billion in investment and financing for American projects.Japan and the U.S. also agreed this week to proceed with a semiconductor manufacturing project in New York under their strategic investment initiative. The project has an estimated cost of $10 billion, with construction scheduled to begin by the end of 2026.Taiwan has yet to announce a construction schedule, identify participating suppliers or disclose when the Texas complex might become operational. The Ministry of Economic Affairs said further details would be provided later.

title: Fossilized blood vessels found in 66-million-year-old dinosaur bone
content: Scientists have unearthed rare fossilized blood vessels inside the broken rib of Scotty, the largest known Tyrannosaurus rex, using neutron imaging to peek inside the 66-million-year-old bone without damaging it.The discovery provides a detailed view into how the dinosaur’s body responded to injury before its death and demonstrates how neutron imaging can reveal soft tissues that are rarely preserved in fossils.Researchers from the University of Regina in Canada combined neutron imaging with advanced X-ray techniques at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) to create high-resolution 3D images of Scotty’s rib. The procedure allowed them to examine the fossil’s internal structure while leaving the rare preserved tissues intact.“It’s like winning the lottery,” said Mauricio Barbi, professor of physics at the University of Regina. “Scotty’s rib contains a vast network of mineralized blood vessels that has never before been observed in a fossil.”Marshy water preserves blood flow Soft tissues such as blood vessels usually disappear during decay long before fossilization occurs, making Scotty’s rib an extraordinary exception.According to the researchers, the dinosaur suffered a broken rib during its lifetime. As the injury healed, iron-rich blood flowed into the damaged area and formed new blood vessels to repair the bone. Before the healing process was complete, however, Scotty died in what scientists believe was a salty marsh. The environment slowed decomposition, allowing the delicate vascular network to survive long enough to become fossilized.Neutrons capture soft tissuesThe team said neutron imaging was highly valuable for this study as it is extremely sensitive to light elements, enabling them to spot subtle remnants of preserved soft tissue that are difficult to identify using conventional imaging methods alone.“Every fossil is a tiny snapshot of the past,” said Jerit Mitchell, a doctoral candidate in physics at the University of Regina who leads the project.The researchers first detected evidence of fossilized blood vessels in Scotty’s rib in 2020 using micro-computed tomography and synchrotron X-ray imaging at the Canadian Light Source. Those studies confirmed preserved soft tissue and helped scientists examine the healing process on microscopic scales.Seeking additional evidence, the team turned to ORNL’s neutron facilities in April 2026. They used the Multimodal Advanced Radiography Station (MARS) at the High Flux Isotope Reactor to image smaller specimens, including fossilized scales and amber. At the same time, the Virtual Environment for Neutron Sciences (VENUS) instrument at the Spallation Neutron Source generated detailed 3D images of larger fossils, including Scotty’s rib.The neutron data not only confirmed the earlier X-ray findings but also revealed new evidence without altering the ancient specimen.“Neutrons not only corroborated what we found with synchrotron radiation techniques that led to the discovery of blood vessels in Scotty’s rib, but they also proved to be a highly valuable addition to our current studies in search of soft tissue preservation in fossils,” said Marcella Berg, assistant professor of physics at the University of Regina in a press statement.Unlike X-rays, which excel at imaging dense materials such as bone, neutrons are especially effective at detecting light elements, including hydrogen. Scientists liken the difference to comparing an MRI, which highlights soft tissues, with an X-ray that emphasizes skeletal structures.In the future, the team plans to investigate pathologies in fossils and compare differences in modern species by neutron imaging with X-ray techniques.“There are more fossils than you think sitting in collections, hiding secrets from millions of years ago,” Mitchell said. “Putting them in a synchrotron or neutron source allows us to make new discoveries about ancient life like never before.”

title: US rival's 3,000-ton submarine launched two strategic cruise missiles
content: North Korea has announced the successful test-firing of two types of strategic cruise missiles in the East Sea. The development signals progress in North Korea’s efforts to strengthen its submarine-based military capabilities and expand its nuclear deterrence strategy.The missiles were launched on October 14, and the test was reportedly designed to assess the operational readiness of underwater combat systems and improve the navy’s ability to carry out strategic missions, according to North Korea.Missiles may have been fired from Hero Kim Kun Ok submarineThe launch has drawn attention because military experts believe the missiles may have been fired from the Hero Kim Kun Ok, a submarine in the 3,000-ton class that North Korea unveiled in September 2023. However, the precise launch platform has not been independently confirmed.North Korea described the Hero Kim Kun Ok as one of the navy’s key offensive assets when it was unveiled in 2023. At the time, leader Kim Jong un highlighted the need to equip the navy with nuclear weapons, underlining Pyongyang’s intention to strengthen its maritime deterrence capabilities.If the latest launch did take place from this submarine, it would suggest that North Korea is continuing to explore ways to integrate advanced missile systems with its expanding naval capabilities.The announcement follows an earlier submarine-launched cruise missile test in January 2024, when Pyongyang said it had fired Pulhwasal-3-31 strategic cruise missiles from the 2,000-ton-class 8.24 Yongung submarine. Spokesperson for South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, Captain Jang Do-young, stated that the military had persistently tracked the activity using multiple surveillance assets. He declined to disclose further operational details, citing confidentiality arrangements with the United States.Submarine-based strategic cruise missilesSubmarine-launched systems are particularly significant because they can introduce additional uncertainty into regional defense calculations. Their effectiveness, however, depends on factors such as the operational reliability of the submarine, missile performance, communications, navigation and the ability to deploy the weapons under realistic conditions.North Korea’s public announcements alone do not establish how successfully these capabilities could be employed in an actual conflict.The possibility of submarine-based strategic cruise missiles adds another dimension to the security challenges facing regional powers. It may require continued attention to maritime surveillance, early-warning systems and coordination among security partners.The cruise missile test comes amid continued efforts by North Korea to advance its missile technology and strengthen its military deterrence posture.Earlier in the same week, North Korea reported testing tactical ballistic missiles from the area around the capital, directing them towards the East Sea. North Korean state media said that test was intended to verify technical improvements to an important component of its weapons systems.As North Korea continues to pursue advanced missile and naval systems, developments in submarine-launched weapons are likely to remain an important issue in the broader security environment of Northeast Asia.

title: Your Bones May Hold a Hidden Clue to Blood Cancer Survival
content:
Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of blood cancers in which the bone marrow fails to produce enough healthy blood cells. Most common in older adults, these disorders can cause anemia, fatigue, frequent infections, and excessive bleeding. Some cases can progress to acute myeloid leukemia, an aggressive form of blood cancer. Credit: Stock
For people with blood cancers called myelodysplastic syndromes, osteoporosis may hold an overlooked clue to survival, a three-year observational study suggests.
In blood cancers that develop in the bone marrow, an important clue to a patient’s survival may lie in the bones themselves. Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), a group of cancers that primarily affect older adults, interfere with the body’s ability to produce healthy blood cells.
Treatment typically focuses on managing anemia, monitoring blood counts, and providing transfusions when necessary. However, new research suggests that bone health, an often-overlooked aspect of MDS care, may reveal important information about patients’ overall health and prognosis.
In a three-year study involving 111 patients with MDS and 84 age-matched control participants, researchers found that people with MDS had significantly lower bone density at the outset and continued to lose bone mass over time. More notably, patients who already had osteoporosis at the beginning of the study also had poorer overall survival. Although the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship, they point to a potentially important connection between bone deterioration and blood cancer outcomes.
“In patients with MDS, the bone-aging process seems to be sped up,” says Prof. Lorenz Hofbauer, director of the University Center for Healthy Aging at Dresden University Hospital.
Analyzed on ice – Stem cells are stored in liquid nitrogen at −196 degrees Celsius and examined for the BOHEME study. Credit: Amac Garbe
MDS becomes more common with age
MDS is among the most common cancers of the blood-forming system. Several thousand people receive an MDS diagnosis in Germany each year. Its incidence rises from approximately 4 to 5 cases per 100,000 people in the general population to more than 30 per 100,000 among people older than 70.
“The results are crucial to our understanding of aging processes,” says Hofbauer. “MDS occurs primarily in elderly individuals, precisely during a phase of life in which bone mass, muscle strength, and physical reserves also decline. Often, there is a chronic, subtle inflammatory process present without there being any apparent cause or infection. In addition, MDS is frequently associated with heart attacks and Alzheimer’s disease.”
Prof. Lorenz Hofbauer. Credit: National Center For Tumor Diseases Dresden
A genetic clue connects blood and bone
Within blood-forming cells, a specific mutation in the DNMT3A gene was associated with lower bone density, providing another connection for researchers to investigate between blood formation and bone health. Participants with low bone density or osteoporosis were also more likely to have low calcium levels.
Hofbauer initiated BoHemE in 2016 with Prof. Uwe Platzbecker, Chief Medical Officer of Dresden University Hospital and a specialist in hematology and oncology. The study involved Dresden and Leipzig University Hospitals, along with other partners in Germany.
The findings open opportunities to investigate how blood formation, aging, and bone metabolism influence one another. This is a systems medicine approach, which examines relationships among biological systems and clinical diseases. Collaboration among specialists in blood disorders, bone health, orthopedics, trauma surgery, computer science, and evidence-based medicine could help uncover further connections and support both research and patient care, particularly for older adults with complex conditions.
“The message of the BoHemE study is clear: If you want to treat MDS comprehensively, you should also keep an eye on bone health,” says Hofbauer.
“Strong bones, a high degree of mobility, and a maintained quality of life are part of a healthy aging process and should be systematically taken into account during the diagnosis and ongoing management of MDS. The Osteoporosis Center at Dresden University Hospital provides suitable treatment options for the individualized management of bone diseases in MDS patients.”
Reference: “Bone health in myelodysplastic neoplasms: results from the prospective longitudinal BoHemE study” by Heike Weidner, Elena Tsourdi, Anne Sophie Platzbecker, Martina Rauner, Ulrike Baschant, Maria G. title: Scientists Discover an Unexpected Problem With a Cancer Drug Already in Human Trials
content:
Researchers have discovered that an experimental cancer drug may work through an unexpected biological mechanism, challenging assumptions about its anticancer effects. Credit: Stock
Earlier cancer studies may need a second look after researchers found that a drug acts mainly on an unexpected target.
An experimental cancer drug already being tested in patients appears to work mainly by blocking a different biological target from the one it was developed to inhibit. The finding emerged from brain cancer research that called into question how the drug, zavondemstat, and a closely related research compound, QC6352, produce their anticancer effects.
Both compounds were developed to treat cancers such as colorectal, pancreatic, and prostate cancer by targeting KDM4, a family of proteins that can help cancer cells grow and spread when overactive. The new investigation explored their potential against glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive form of brain cancer.
“We tested these compounds to investigate whether they could potentially be repurposed for glioblastoma treatment,” said lead author Professor Lenka Munoz of the University of Sydney School of Medical Sciences and Charles Perkins Centre.
“When we tested other KDM4 inhibitors, we found they did not reproduce the anti-cancer effects observed with QC6352.
“If blocking KDM4 was driving those effects, we would have expected the other inhibitors to behave similarly. Instead, the results suggested QC6352 was acting through a different mechanism.”
Cutting the supply of DNA building blocks
To trace that mechanism, the team used patient-derived glioblastoma stem cells, tumor models, and a series of genetic, mechanistic, and molecular experiments. The University of Sydney led the research in collaboration with Goethe University, Oxford University, and the Institute of Cancer Research, London. The results were published in
Nature Chemical Biology
“Our study found much of the anti-cancer activity of these compounds is driven by blocking DHODH rather than KDM4,” Munoz said.
DHODH is an enzyme that cancer cells rely on to produce molecules needed for rapid growth. Blocking it interferes with the supply of materials needed for DNA production.
“We can think of DHODH as a machine producing bricks needed to build new DNA. If you switch off the machine, the cell starts running out of bricks and can no longer efficiently copy its DNA and keep dividing,” Munoz said.
The findings point to DHODH inhibition as a possible approach to treating glioblastoma. Several drugs that target the enzyme are already being investigated for other cancers, raising the possibility that they could eventually be tested in patients with brain cancer. The current findings come from cells and tumor models, however, and do not establish that these drugs would benefit patients with glioblastoma.
Earlier KDM4 findings may need reinterpreting
The implications also extend to experiments that have used QC6352 to investigate what KDM4 does in cancer.
“Researchers around the world have used QC6352 as a leading tool to study KDM4 biology, while the related drug zavondemstat progressed into clinical trials based on the same understanding,” Munoz said.
If effects attributed to KDM4 inhibition were largely caused by blocking DHODH, earlier studies using QC6352 may need to be reinterpreted. To help researchers distinguish the two, the team developed new compounds that inhibit KDM4 without affecting DHODH. Those compounds could allow scientists to investigate KDM4’s role more accurately.
A mistaken target can misdirect trials
For zavondemstat’s ongoing clinical development, the findings raise questions about whether trials are being designed around the biological process responsible for much of the drug’s activity.
“Getting a drug’s mechanism wrong can lead to poorly designed clinical trials, inappropriate patient selection and years of research focused on the wrong biological target,” Munoz said.
“There are well-known examples of cancer drugs advancing through large clinical trials before researchers realized they were not working through the mechanism originally proposed.
“Our study shows this is not just a historical problem but one still happening today. Greater rigor is needed to ensure we understand exactly how potential treatments work before they move into clinical testing.
“Establishing a drug’s true mechanism early can protect patients, prevent wasted research effort, and help ensure what limited funding we have is directed towards genuinely promising treatments.”

Saxton, Jennifer R. Baker, Zhihe Lei, Matthew T. O. Holland, Paul E. Brennan, Mathias Francois, Andreas Kraemer, Susanne Mueller, Yuchen Feng, Paul Workman and Lenka Munoz, 6 October 2026,
Nature Chemical Biology

title: SpaceX Dragon Delivers Groundbreaking Science and Solar Arrays to ISS
content:
A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft approaches the International Space Station moments before docking to the Harmony module’s space-facing port on October 15, 2026. Credit: NASA+
SpaceX has delivered tiny brain models, 3D heart tissue, and artificial retina technology to the space station in a mission that could open new doors for medical research on Earth.
SpaceX’s Dragon spacecraft successfully arrived at the International Space Station on October 15, docking at 10:27 a.m. EDT with the space-facing port of the station’s Harmony module. The spacecraft brought more than 6,300 pounds of food, equipment, and other essential supplies for the Expedition 75 crew. The delivery marks SpaceX’s 35th commercial resupply mission to the orbiting laboratory under its contract with NASA.
New Solar Arrays and Advanced Medical Research
Among the cargo is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs), which astronauts are expected to install later this fall. These arrays will expand the station’s ability to generate electricity from sunlight.
Dragon also delivered equipment for several ambitious scientific investigations that could lead to important advances in medicine and materials science. One experiment will explore manufacturing
artificial retinas
in microgravity, with the long-term goal of helping restore eyesight on Earth. Another will use
3D heart tissue models
to support the development of large-scale drug testing during future space missions.
Additional research will examine how a
new type of glass
forms in the weightless environment of space. Scientists will also study
brain organoids
, miniature models of brain tissue that could help identify potential treatment targets for neurological conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and multiple sclerosis.
Dragon’s Return to Earth
Dragon is expected to remain docked at the space station until mid-November. It will then transport time-sensitive scientific research and other cargo back to Earth, concluding its mission with a splashdown off the California coast.
The spacecraft began its journey on October 13 at 6:33 a.m. EDT, launching aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

title: The Milky Way’s Monster Black Hole May Be Sacrificing Its Own Energy To Power Cosmic Rays
content:
In this artist’s conception, the black hole at the center of our galaxy is surrounded by a hot disk of accreting material. Blue lines trace magnetic fields. Credit: M. Weiss / Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics
The Milky Way’s central black hole could lose mass by powering escaping particles, and new calculations suggest how astronomers might detect the process.
The supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way may be accelerating particles to energies far beyond anything achievable in Earth’s most powerful particle accelerators. A new theoretical study suggests that Sagittarius A*, a black hole roughly four million times the Sun’s mass, could accomplish this by transferring some of its rotational energy directly to protons.
The researchers estimate that these particles could reach energies of several petaelectronvolts (PeV), equivalent to several quadrillion electron volts. That would make Sagittarius A* a possible Galactic PeVatron, a natural particle accelerator capable of producing some of the most energetic cosmic rays in our galaxy.
How Black Holes Could Power Extreme Particle Acceleration
Most of the intense radiation associated with actively feeding black holes originates from surrounding matter rather than from the black holes themselves. However, physicist Roger Penrose proposed in 1969 that rotating black holes could also surrender some of their own energy through a mechanism known as the Penrose process.
This process operates in the ergosphere, a region where the black hole’s rotation twists spacetime so strongly that everything must move in the direction of its spin.
Think of the black hole as a giant, rapidly spinning merry-go-round that drags the surrounding spacetime along with it. Under certain conditions, a particle entering this region can split apart, with one fragment falling into the black hole while the other escapes with more energy than the original particle possessed.
The extra energy comes from the black hole’s own rotation, much like an object gaining an extra boost from a spinning merry-go-round. A more powerful variation, called the magnetic Penrose process (MPP), uses magnetic fields to transfer this rotational energy to charged particles much more efficiently, potentially launching them into space at extraordinarily high energies.
Schematic of how decaying particles can extract energy from a black hole. Credit: Cermeño, et al.
In the new study, researchers modeled neutrons produced by nuclear reactions in the hot gas surrounding Sagittarius A*. Some neutrons could enter the ergosphere and decay into protons, electrons, and antineutrinos. The resulting charged particles would interact with the magnetic field, potentially allowing protons to escape with enormous amounts of energy.
“Our results strengthen the interpretation of Sgr A* as a candidate Galactic PeVatron,” the researchers write in their study.
Could Gamma Rays Reveal the Hidden Process?
These accelerated protons would travel outward and collide with dense gas in the Central Molecular Zone surrounding the Galactic center. Such collisions can produce gamma rays and neutrinos, providing potential observational evidence of the mechanism.
Astronomers have already detected very-high-energy gamma rays from the Galactic center, but their precise origins remain uncertain. Tracing the source of cosmic rays is particularly difficult because their electric charges cause magnetic fields to bend their trajectories. Gamma rays, by comparison, travel without being deflected by those fields, making them valuable for locating regions of extreme particle acceleration.
The researchers calculated that the magnetic Penrose process could produce distinctive features in the gamma-ray energy spectrum and contribute to emission already observed by H.E.S.S. and HAWC. Their models predict signals within the expected sensitivity of the planned Southern Wide-field Gamma-ray Observatory (SWGO), with the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) potentially able to test some scenarios.
“Our results indicate that SWGO should be capable of probing all the scenarios that we are considering in this work,” the researchers write.
References: “Sgr A* as a Galactic PeVatron: Multimessenger Signatures of the Magnetic Penrose Process” by Marina Cermeño, Pedro De la Torre Luque, Cristina Fernández-Suárez, Viviana Gammaldi, Enrique Mier-Alonso, María J. Rodríguez, Miguel Á. Sánchez-Conde and Jaume Zuriaga-Puig, September 2, 2026,
DOI: 2609.04051

title: NASA Is About to Investigate What Lies Beneath a Giant Hole on the Moon
content:
Artist’s concept of a potential lunar cave beneath the Marius Hills region of the Moon. NASA-backed scientists plan to investigate whether a vast lava tube lies hidden below the surface, potentially revealing clues about the Moon’s ancient volcanic history. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
NASA is backing a search for a hidden lunar cave that could reveal how ancient volcanic activity shaped the Moon.
Scientists have gathered compelling evidence from lunar orbit for caves and lava tubes beneath the Moon’s surface, places that could one day shelter astronauts from radiation and extreme temperature swings.
NASA has selected a Planetary Science Institute (PSI)-led project to investigate whether a potentially large cave extends beyond the opening of the Marius Hill Pit (MHP).
Sizing up a possible lunar cave
A lander and rover will carry the instruments for the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI. Ground-penetrating radar will probe buried structures with radio waves, while seismic sensors will record how deliberately generated vibrations travel through the ground. The team will combine those readings with gravity measurements from a gravimeter and camera images of the surface and pit walls to investigate the surrounding material and estimate the size of any void it finds.
“It’s long been a desire of mine to reintroduce intentional active-source seismic methods to planetary science, as it has essentially not been done since the Apollo astronauts conducted the first seismic surveys on the Moon,” said GIMLI leader Than Putzig, PSI Associate Director and Senior Scientist. “Combining that method with ground-penetrating radar and gravity measurements makes it all the more exciting, as these methods together will allow us to get a much better understanding of subsurface properties — including the anticipated detection of a lava tube extending away from the Marius Hills pit.”
Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, will build much of the equipment, including instrumentation for the active-source seismic system, gravimeter, and cameras. As PSI’s commercial partner, the company will also provide project management services, integrate all the instruments onto the lander and rover, and jointly lead their lunar surface operations with PSI.
The Marius Hills Pit (MHP) on the surface of the Moon. MHP will be studied by PSI-led GIMLI, through the NASA PRISM program, to investigate a possible lava tube beneath the surface. Credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University
The Norwegian Space Agency will supply the ground-penetrating radar and partner with PSI on its work. Co-investigators from Boise State University, Johns Hopkins University, the Lunar and Planetary Institute, and the University of Oslo will also contribute to the project.
NASA will fund GIMLI through its Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program, which sends scientific instruments to the Moon aboard spacecraft supplied by Commercial Lunar Payloads Services (CLPS) initiative providers. A CLPS provider will supply the lander and rover.
“GIMLI represents the type of ambitious planetary science that PSI was built to pursue,” said PSI Director and CEO Amanda Hendrix. “Than and his team are taking a scientific question we’ve been studying from orbit and have developed a way to investigate it directly on the Moon. We’re excited to have PSI leading this effort and to be partnering with NASA and Honeybee Robotics to learn more about the Moon and its volcanic past.”
A volcanic record in the pit’s walls
MHP is a large hole in one of the Moon’s most volcanically diverse regions, and its walls expose layers of lava flows and regolith, the loose material covering the surface, that usually lie hidden underground. Studying these layers could reveal how lava traveled through the region during its long volcanic history and whether lengthy intervals separated eruptions. If GIMLI finds a cave or lava tube, its interior could preserve further evidence of the ancient volcanic activity that may have formed it.
“Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the Moon,” explained Gareth Morgan, PSI Senior Scientist and Deputy Principal Investigator on the GIMLI program. “Lava tubes are a common feature of basaltic volcanism on Earth, so identifying them on the Moon means we could use knowledge of such terrestrial caves to better understand lunar history.”
Even if GIMLI finds no cave or lava tube, its measurements of the surrounding subsurface could help explain how the pit formed and clarify the geology and volcanic history of the site.
The project will be funded through NASA’s Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program, which sends scientific instruments to the Moon on spacecraft provided by the Commercial Lunar Payloads Services (CLPS) initiative providers.

title: A Virus Gives Itself Away the Moment It Attacks
content:
Bacteriophage (red) infecting and killing E.coli (blue) over three stages. Credit: David S. Goodsell, RCSB Protein Data Bank, and Scripps Research. doi: 10.2210/rcsb_pdb/goodsell-gallery-048
Researchers have found the trigger behind a powerful bacterial defense against viruses.
Viruses that prey on bacteria could become an increasingly important tool for treating bacterial infections, particularly as antibiotic resistance makes some infections harder to control. These viruses, known as bacteriophages (phages), can infect and destroy harmful bacteria without damaging human cells.
Using phages as treatments, however, comes with a major challenge. Bacteria are not defenseless against viruses. They possess their own immune systems, and understanding those defenses could help scientists design phage therapies that are better able to overcome them.
Researchers have now uncovered a surprising mechanism that bacteria use to recognize an incoming viral attack. Instead of simply sensing viral genetic material, bacteria can detect the activity of an enzyme the virus itself needs. When that viral enzyme cuts an important sensor molecule inside the bacterium, it sets off an immune response.
The discovery could ultimately help scientists develop more effective phage therapies capable of avoiding or overcoming bacterial immune defenses.
“This is one of the most common forms of bacterial immunity, so when we finally figured it out, it was a total eureka moment,” says Sam Hobbs, PhD, assistant professor of biochemistry at University of Utah Health and the first author on a paper describing the research.
The results are published in
Science.
Sam Hobbs, PhD. Credit: Sam Hobbs
Bacteria’s Last Resort Against Viruses
The immune system involved is known as CBASS. When activated, it can trigger an extreme defensive strategy: the infected bacterium kills itself before the invading virus has a chance to multiply and spread into neighboring bacterial cells.
Because activating this response costs the bacterium its life, the system needs a reliable way to determine that a genuine viral attack is underway.
Hobbs and his colleagues found that the bacterial sensor responds to a molecule that the invading virus depends on for survival. Some phages produce enzymes called proteases, which cut and break down proteins.
“Certain kinds of phages have a protein called a protease, which degrades other proteins,” he explains. “We found that the protease from the phage actually acts directly on the host protein, and that is the signal that turns on the whole signaling pathway.”
In other words, the virus effectively reveals itself through one of the molecular tools it uses during infection. When its protease cuts the bacterial protein, that action serves as the warning signal that activates CBASS.
A Surprising Viral Trigger
The mechanism differs sharply from related antiviral defenses that recognize the genetic material of invading viruses. Rather than detecting viral DNA or RNA, this bacterial system senses the activity of a viral protein.
“This is a totally new mechanism for how these host proteins are activated,” Hobbs says. “I never would have guessed that this was the way it was going to work.”
Understanding this molecular trigger could be especially important for improving phage therapy. If researchers know exactly how bacteria recognize certain phages, they may be able to develop therapeutic viruses that are less likely to activate those defenses.
That could make bacteriophages more effective against harmful bacteria, including strains that have developed resistance to conventional antibiotics.
An Ancient Link to Human Immunity
The findings may also have implications beyond bacteria. CBASS is related to an immune pathway found in humans, suggesting that fundamental elements of this antiviral defense have extremely ancient evolutionary origins.
According to the researchers, the connection indicates that the pathway has existed at least since the distant common ancestor shared by bacteria and humans.
Bacteria also reproduce and evolve rapidly, making them useful systems for investigating basic questions about immunity. Scientists can study immune mechanisms in bacteria relatively quickly and then test whether similar principles apply in biological models that are more closely related to humans.
“The fact that these systems are conserved between bacteria and humans suggests that they’ve been maintained in these different organisms for that entire evolutionary trajectory,” Hobbs says. “The cells are telling us that this is a really important pathway because they’ve maintained it for billions of years. It’s incredibly fascinating, and it’s a cool window into what’s important in maintaining the ability to fight viruses.”

as “Phage proteases activate CBASS antiphage immunity.”

title: Scientists Discover a Terrifying New Dinosaur Hidden for 100 Years
content:
An artist’s illustration of the new theropod dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina (center of the image), in its ecosystem on the Isle of Wight, United Kingdom in the Early Cretaceous (around 120 million years ago). It lived in what was likely a seasonally wet-to-dry floodplain environment and is surrounded by other dinosaurs including large long-necked rebbachisaurid sauropods (directly behind Invictibellatrix, center) and relatives of Iguanodon (right). A spinosaurid theropod, potentially the apex predator of the time, fishes (left). Invictibellatrix has just caught and is consuming two small mammals. Gymnosperms dominate the environment as flowering plants (angiosperms) were not common at this time. Other reptiles including relatives to modern lizards, crocodiles and turtles enjoy the warm Early Cretaceous weather of the UK. Credit: Sergey Krasovskiy and Pedro Salas
A dinosaur fossil that sat unnoticed in a museum collection for nearly a century has turned out to belong to a previously unknown predator with enormous curved claws. The animal, roughly the size of a large tiger, lived in what is now Britain about 120 million years ago.
The discovery was made by a research team led by University College London (UCL) using a fossil originally found on the Isle of Wight. Described in the journal
Royal Society Open Science
, the dinosaur is the first known European member of a mysterious group of meat-eating dinosaurs called megaraptorans.
These agile predators walked on two legs and were closely related to tyrannosaurs, including the famous
Tyrannosaurus rex
. However, their hunting strategy was very different. Rather than relying primarily on powerful jaws, megaraptorans had relatively narrow heads and used their muscular arms and large, curved claws to capture prey.
Some eventually grew into enormous predators comparable in size to the largest tyrannosaurs. The newly identified species, however, was among the earliest and smallest known members of the group. It lived during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 120 million years ago.
Researchers named the dinosaur
Invictibellatrix amberina
. The genus name
Invictibellatrix
translates to “unconquered female warrior,” recognizing the group’s eventual rise to dominance as massive apex predators.
Remarkably, the fossil consists of a fragment from the back of the dinosaur’s skull that entered the Natural History Museum’s collection in 1924. Despite its scientific importance, it remained largely overlooked until researchers examined it nearly 100 years later.
Fossil of newly identified theropod dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina. The oval hole is where the brain would have been. The fossil was acquired by the Natural History Museum in 1924. Credit: The Trustees of the Natural History Museum, London
A Dinosaur That Might Have Been More Dangerous Than T. Rex
Lead author Dr. Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) explained what the animal may have looked like and how it hunted.
“Based on what we know about its closest relatives,
Invictibellatrix
would have been three to four meters long and just over a meter and a half in height – about as tall as a human. It would likely have had feathers, and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long. It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals – occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today.
“It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a
We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A
would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.
“It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight – who knows what else is waiting to be discovered.”
Although humans did not exist when these dinosaurs lived, Morrison’s comparison illustrates how the smaller predator’s size and hunting behavior might have made it particularly dangerous to human-sized prey.
A Missing Link in the History of Giant Predators
Megaraptorans remain among the least understood groups of large carnivorous dinosaurs, largely because their fossils are so rare. For years, scientists have struggled to piece together where they originated and how they spread across the ancient continents.
One leading theory suggests that megaraptorans first evolved in Asia before traveling through Europe and eventually reaching Gondwana (including present-day Africa, South America and Antarctica). There, some species became apex predators, meaning they occupied the very top of their ecosystems’ food chains.
Until this discovery, however, an important piece of evidence was missing. No megaraptoran fossils had ever been identified in Europe, leaving a major gap in the proposed migration route.
The discovery of
Invictibellatrix
now provides direct evidence that these dinosaurs inhabited Europe.
Co-author Charlie Scherer, a PhD student at UCL Earth Sciences, said: “This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south.”
CT Scans Reveal a Previously Unknown Dinosaur
To investigate the fossil, the researchers used computed tomography, or CT scanning, a technique that uses X-rays to examine the internal structure of an object without damaging it.
The scans allowed the team to produce a detailed 3D reconstruction of the skull fragment, along with a digital model of the internal space that once housed the dinosaur’s brain.
They then compared these structures with skulls and braincases from other carnivorous dinosaurs, including tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors, and various other predators that walked on two legs.
Several unusual anatomical details helped distinguish the specimen from previously identified species. Among them were an oval opening where the spinal cord connected to the brain and a distinctive crest shaped like an hourglass.
Together, these features convinced the researchers that the fossil represented a new dinosaur species.
Computer algorithms provided further support. By comparing the fossil’s anatomical characteristics with those of other dinosaurs, the researchers repeatedly found that it belonged within the megaraptoran group.
How Megaraptors Spread Across the Ancient World
The researchers also investigated the evolutionary history of megaraptorans and how their geographic range changed over millions of years.
Using mathematical models, they combined evidence from known fossils, evolutionary relationships between dinosaur species, ancient geography, and prehistoric climate conditions.
Their results suggest that megaraptorans were distributed widely across the world during the Early Cretaceous (i.e., at the time of
Invictibellatrix
However, their fortunes appear to have changed dramatically over the following tens of millions of years.
Meanwhile, megaraptorans in the southern supercontinent of Gondwana became some of the most formidable predators of their time. Several evolved into enormous hunters equipped with curved claws reaching 35 cm (14 in) in length.
One particularly impressive example was
Maip macrothorax
, discovered in what is now Argentina. Scientists estimate that this giant carnivore measured approximately nine to 10 meters long and weighed as much as an elephant.
Exactly why megaraptorans disappeared from northern regions remains uncertain. The study did not establish a definitive cause, but changes in climate, shifting environmental conditions, and competition from other large predators, including tyrannosaurs, may have contributed to their decline.
A Century-Old Museum Fossil Reveals a New Species
The fossil that revealed
Invictibellatrix amberina
was originally collected by amateur paleontologist Reginald Walter Tooley near the base of a cliff on the southwestern coast of the Isle of Wight.
Tooley was an exceptionally productive fossil collector who discovered more than 1,000 specimens. Following his death, those fossils became part of the Natural History Museum’s collections.
For nearly a century, the skull fragment remained among those historic specimens without its true identity being recognized.
Professor Paul Barrett, the study’s senior author from the Natural History Museum, emphasized that even extensively explored fossil sites can continue to produce unexpected discoveries.
“Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as
Invictibellatrix,
have been particularly elusive.
“Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made.”
The dinosaur’s name also carries a message beyond its evolutionary significance.
In their paper, the researchers explained that
Invictibellatrix
was chosen to “give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in face of such odds.”
The species name
amberina
refers both to the amber preserved in the rocks where the fossil originated and to the female given name.
The discovery highlights the continuing scientific importance of museum collections. Even specimens gathered generations ago can contain valuable clues about prehistoric life, and some may still represent species that scientists have never recognized.
Reference: “A new megaraptoran dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous Wessex Formation, UK, and its implications for theropod evolution and biogeography” by Cassius Morrison, Charlie R. Scherer, Philip Mannion, Laura B. Porro, Brett Clark, Daniel D. Folkes and Paul M. Barrett, 14 October 2026,
Royal Society Open Science
DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260937
The research received funding from the Palaeontographical Society, the Royal Society, and UKRI.

title: NASA Captures a Strange Formation on Earth With a Surprising Lunar Connection
content:
A giant patch of Moon-like rock stands out in southern Madagascar, revealing an ancient geological connection between Earth and the Moon. Credit: NASA
A NASA astronaut captured a stunning 600-million-year-old rock formation in Madagascar that shares a surprising geological connection with the Moon.
A striking patch of bright rock in southern Madagascar has an unexpected connection to the Moon. Surrounded by rocks that were twisted and stretched by ancient geological forces, the formation contains anorthosite, the same type of rock that makes up much of the Moon’s bright highlands.
Viewed from space, the unusual formation stands out against Madagascar’s dry, rugged landscape. Anorthosite is an igneous rock found in abundance on the Moon, where it forms the highly reflective regions known as the lunar highlands. These pale regions are so prominent that they can be distinguished from Earth without a telescope.
Although closely associated with the Moon, anorthosite is also found in several places on Earth, including eastern Canada, Scandinavia, southern India, and Madagascar. In southern Madagascar, it forms a distinctive, roughly circular feature that is particularly noticeable in photographs taken from orbit.
NASA Astronaut Captures Ancient Moon-Like Rock Formation
On August 28, 2026, an astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the Saririaky anorthosite massif, a large body of rock exposed at Earth’s surface.
Anorthosite forms when magma cools and solidifies beneath the ground, allowing relatively large mineral crystals to develop. Rocks produced through this process are known as intrusive igneous rocks.
Scientists believe
the Saririaky massif originated during the late Precambrian, making it at least 600 million years old. Today, the exposed formation extends across approximately 100 square kilometers (40 square miles).
The surrounding landscape provides evidence of the enormous geological forces that have acted on the region since the rock formed. Researchers have
identified
the massif within a
ductile shear zone
, an area where rocks were gradually stretched and distorted under intense heat and pressure.
These conditions caused the surrounding rocks to undergo metamorphism, changing their structure and producing long, roughly parallel patterns that extend from north to south.
Ancient Continental Collisions Reshaped Madagascar
Geologists suspect that this dramatic transformation occurred during the assembly of Gondwana, the enormous supercontinent that once united landmasses now separated by oceans.
As portions of present-day Africa, India, Madagascar, Australia, and Antarctica collided, tremendous pressure deformed the rocks caught between them. The resulting geological structures preserve evidence of those ancient continental movements.
Some researchers have suggested that a second anorthosite massif, located approximately 60 kilometers (40 miles) north of Saririaky within the same shear zone, may once have been connected to it.
According to this hypothesis, the immense forces associated with continental collision stretched and separated the original rock body. This process can produce a structure known as boudinage, in which a relatively resistant layer of rock is pulled apart into distinct segments as the surrounding material deforms.
How Earth’s Moon-Like Rocks Reveal Lunar History
Beyond their importance to understanding Earth’s geological past, anorthosite formations also provide scientists with valuable opportunities to investigate the Moon’s earliest history.
The Moon’s anorthosite rocks are more than 4 billion years old. Scientists believe they formed when the young Moon was covered by a vast ocean of molten rock. As this magma cooled, anorthosite crystallized and became a major component of the Moon’s outer crust.
Samples collected by Apollo astronauts have given researchers direct evidence of these ancient lunar materials. However, because the available Moon rocks are limited, scientists also examine similar formations on Earth to better understand their composition and formation.
One especially useful comparison comes from the Beartooth Mountains in Montana, where anorthosite closely resembles its lunar counterpart in chemical composition.
Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-85249 was taken on August 28, 2026, using a Nikon Z9 digital camera equipped with a 400-millimeter lens. The image was captured by an astronaut from the Expedition 75 crew and supplied by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. It has been cropped, adjusted to enhance contrast, and processed to remove lens artifacts.
